On Monday 27 April 2026, US service members at Naval Support Activity Bahrain began receiving WhatsApp messages on their personal phones. Signed Handala. The text:

"Your identities are fully known to our missile units. Soon you will be targeted by our Shahed drones and Kheibar missiles. We suggest you call your families now and say your final goodbyes."

The next day Handala — the cover identity for Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security, tracked as Storm-0842 — published the claimed personal details of 2,379 named US Marines. Rank. Unit. Home address. Family details. Daily commute. Shopping habits. Nightly leisure activities.

The security community's first instinct was to qualify the incident: the data was likely scraped from data brokers and social media rather than gathered from secure systems. That qualification reaches the opposite conclusion from the one intended.

If the targeting package for 2,379 named Marines was assembled from commercial sources rather than a breach, the threat is more serious, not less.

It means the intelligence collection system that produced personalised missile-threat messages required no exploit, no insider, no nation-state cyber capability, and no access to any classified system. It required a data broker account and a LinkedIn search.

This is the convergence article — the one that ties three previous DSI Chokepoint Doctrine pieces into a single argument:

→ The adtech surveillance piece: USCENTCOM confirmed targeting use of commercial location data, 14 April 2026.
→ The connected vehicle piece: the telemetry every modern car emits.
→ The Handala profile: who the actor is and what they do.

Three commercial data streams. One mosaic assembly. One personalised delivery channel — the most personal device in every Marine's pocket.

The adversary did not hack the military. It bought the data the military permitted its personnel to generate. That is the chokepoint no firewall closes.

If your organisation procures from any of the same data brokers — and most do — the same threat model applies to your executives, your board, and your operational personnel.

Whose name is in your supplier's catalogue this week?

Most people think a ₹600 restaurant meal is a better business than a ₹30 biscuit packet.

But structurally, businesses like Britannia and Nestlé often generate far higher returns with significantly lower capital intensity.

This is NOT truly an apple-to-apple comparison.

FMCG and restaurant businesses solve the same human need — food consumption — but through completely different economic models.

One scales through:
- distribution,
- repeat consumption,
- operating leverage,
- and brand habit.

The other scales through:
- physical expansion,
- service execution,
- customer experience,
- and location economics.

Britannia and Nestlé are already mature giants with limited growth runway.
Meanwhile, India’s QSR and restaurant industry may still be in the early innings of expansion.

The real question is:
Why do some business models structurally generate higher returns on capital than others?

Until you finally think: "Why am I even doing this?"

No one tells you:

➡️ You're burned out because you're attached to the outcome.

Not the work. The outcome.

➡️ If you keep posting for attention, you'll never get enough.

Because attention is unpredictable. It comes and goes. It never stays. 🌟 

So here's what I did differently:

I stopped caring about the metrics.

Not in a "I don't check them" way.

🌟 In a "I don't make decisions based on them" way.

Every post I write, I ask myself one question:

"Is this creating value for someone, or am I just trying to be seen?"

If it's the first one, I post it.

If it's the second one, I scrap it.

And here's what happened:
🤍  My posts actually performed better
🤍  I stopped feeling burned out
🤍 The metrics followed naturally

Because the moment you stop chasing metrics, they actually show up.

Not because of magic.

But because when you're focused on value, your content becomes better.

And that's what attracts engagement.

Start creating for value.
Stay detatched from the outcome.

Divert all your energy into making something useful.

And trust that the metrics will follow.

They always do. 

Are you creating for attention, or creating for value? Let's talk.

Ces derniers jours sur LinkedIn, je vois de plus en plus de publications annonçant la “fin des ERP”.

Selon certains, avec l’IA, Claude Code, Lovable et les nouveaux outils de génération, il deviendrait bientôt inutile d’utiliser des ERP comme Divalto, Odoo, SAP ou Sage.

Honnêtement, je pense que la réalité est beaucoup plus nuancée.

Oui, l’IA va profondément transformer la manière de développer des logiciels.
Et c’est déjà en train de se produire.

Aujourd’hui, on peut :
➡️ développer beaucoup plus vite,
➡️ générer des interfaces en quelques minutes,
➡️ créer des workflows rapidement,
➡️ tester des idées plus facilement,
➡️ automatiser une partie du développement.

C’est une révolution technologique majeure.

Mais il y a une énorme différence entre :
👉 développer une petite application fonctionnelle,
et
👉 construire un ERP complet, robuste et capable de tenir pendant 10 ou 15 ans dans une entreprise.

Un ERP, ce n’est pas juste quelques écrans et une base de données.

C’est :

✔️ des dizaines d’années d’évolution,
✔️ des milliers de cas métiers gérés,
✔️ des contraintes réglementaires,
✔️ des problématiques de sécurité,
✔️ des enjeux de performance,
✔️ des mécanismes de traçabilité,
✔️ de la conformité légale,
✔️ des certifications,
✔️ des montées de version,
✔️ de la maintenance continue,
✔️ de l’interconnexion avec d’autres systèmes,
✔️ et surtout des milliers d’heures de retour terrain.

Développer seul une application avec l’IA n’a jamais été aussi accessible.
Et c’est une excellente chose.

Mais maintenir cette application dans le temps, la sécuriser, la faire évoluer, garantir sa stabilité, sa conformité et sa capacité à accompagner la croissance d’une entreprise… c’est une toute autre histoire.

Je pense que l’IA ne va pas remplacer les ERP.
En revanche, elle va profondément transformer la manière dont ils seront développés, personnalisés et intégrés.

Les éditeurs ERP qui sauront intégrer intelligemment l’IA dans leurs plateformes prendront probablement une énorme avance dans les prochaines années.

Et les intégrateurs ERP devront eux aussi évoluer :
✔️ moins de développement répétitif,
✔️ plus de conseil,
✔️ plus d’architecture,
✔️ plus d’accompagnement métier,
✔️ plus de vision globale des flux et des données.

L’IA va accélérer énormément de choses.
Mais construire un ERP fiable et durable restera encore longtemps un travail d’expérience, de méthode et de compréhension du terrain.

Et vous, pensez-vous que l’IA remplacera réellement les ERP historiques dans les prochaines années ? 👇

Ah, LinkedIn 🌈

All the scrolling of Instagram, but for people with lanyards.

Every second post seems to feature someone who is absolutely delighted to be attending a conference, thrilled to be moderating a panel, or honoured to be speaking at an event.

Maybe they are. Maybe I’ve been attending the wrong conferences all these years…  But if we’re honest, some of us are mostly delighted when the coffee is decent and we make it through the day without volunteering ourselves to sit on yet another steering group. 

This Pride Month, I’ve been thinking about authenticity.

Not corporate authenticity.
Not carefully curated content authenticity.
Not the kind that appears once a year when rainbow logos come out of storage.

You know… actual authenticity. 

The kind where people feel able to show up as themselves, admit when they don’t know something, and occasionally acknowledge that they are not, in fact, delighted by every aspect of professional life.

I’m generally not known for sitting quietly on the fence.

Sometimes that’s served me well.
Sometimes it’s got me into trouble.

But I’ve always believed leadership starts with being genuine. People don’t need polished perfection. They need honesty, integrity, and a reasonable chance that the person they’re talking to is the same person they’d meet over a coffee.

Rainbow logos have their place.

Visibility matters.
Representation matters.
Seeing organisations publicly support LGBT+ people matters.

But perhaps the challenge for all of us is moving from ‘rainbow washing’ visibility for profit to visibility for purpose.

Not asking, “How will this make us look?”

But asking, “How will this help people feel seen, valued and included?”

Belonging is what happens after the social media posts are written. It’s created through everyday conversations, leadership decisions, workplace cultures and communities where people feel able to show up as themselves without feeling the need to edit themselves to belong.

Not just during Pride Month. 
All year round, thanks. 🌈

“Vi hittade dig på LinkedIn.”
Det är en mening som inte hade existerat för två år sedan.

För två år sedan var jag i princip osynlig här. Jag publicerade sällan något, hade ingen tydlig strategi och såg LinkedIn mest som ett digitalt CV.

Sedan började jag dela med mig av det jag faktiskt kan.
Inte sälja. Dela.
Tankar om voice over. Erfarenheter från studion. Små insikter om hur en röst påverkar ett budskap.
Inget av det blev viralt.

Men jag fortsatte ändå.

Inte för att jag hade skickat ett säljmejl.
Inte för att jag hade köpt annonser.
Utan för att jag hade dykt upp regelbundet med något som var relevant för dem.

Det är lätt att tro att synlighet handlar om räckvidd.
Jag tror att det handlar mer om igenkänning.

Och igenkänning bygger förtroende.
Så om du funderar på att börja dela med dig av det du kan - börja.

Du vet aldrig vem som läser idag och hör av sig om sex månader.

🚀 Day 83/100 – LeetCode Daily Challenge

📌 Problem: 3753. Total Waviness of Numbers in Range II
🔗 https://lnkd.in/gSdC8Ugb

💡 Approach:
- The range can be extremely large, making brute-force enumeration impossible.
- Used Digit DP to count numbers and their total waviness efficiently.
- Process digits from left to right while maintaining:
 • Current position
 • Previous digits
 • Tight constraint (whether the prefix matches the limit)
 • Accumulated waviness count
- For each middle digit, determine whether it forms:
 • A peak (greater than both neighbors), or
 • A valley (smaller than both neighbors).
- Memoize DP states to avoid recomputation.
- Compute total waviness from 0 to num2 and subtract the result from 0 to num1−1.

✅ Time Complexity: O(D × States × 10)

✅ Space Complexity: O(States)

Your LinkedIn profile is either a door or a wall. Most are walls.

Here's how you know which one yours is:

A wall profile:
Generic headline that reads like a job title, about section that lists skills instead of telling a story
No recent posts or activity
No clear indication of who you help or how
Makes the visitor work to understand what you do

A door profile:
Headline that says exactly who you help and how
About section that speaks directly to your ideal client or employer
Regular posts that demonstrate your thinking
Clear services or portfolio
Makes the visitor feel like they've already started a conversation

The difference is not talent. It's not experience. It's intentionality.
Most people set up their LinkedIn once and leave it. A door profile is something you build deliberately with your specific audience in mind, updated as you grow.

If someone landed on your profile right now and spent 30 seconds on it, what would they conclude?

That's your answer.

Yesterday, I crossed 10,000 followers on LinkedIn! 🥳

And somewhere along the way, this community became my favourite part of the internet.

10,000 people here now.

Honestly, that means a lot.

Because when I started posting on LinkedIn, I wasn’t trying to become a creator or build an audience.

I just wanted to make ESG and sustainability less overwhelming for businesses that genuinely want to do better, but don’t know where to begin.

And somewhere along the way, 10,000 people stayed for those conversations.

Founders.
ESG professionals.
Teams navigating GHG Accounting and BRSR for the first time.
People trying to understand how sustainability actually works beyond reports and buzzwords.

A few years ago, I probably looked at companies very differently.

During my Master’s in Environmental Economics, we were taught to see companies through a very critical lens, that growth and capitalism often come at the cost of people and the environment.

Then I started working with companies directly.

And my perspective changed.

Most companies are not intentionally trying to do harm.
Many are simply trying to balance business realities while figuring out what responsible growth should actually look like.

That belief became one of the foundations of PlanetaryPlus.

Not as a company that “calls out” businesses, but as someone who can work with them, guide them, and help them move from confusion to clarity. 

And honestly, that’s why this community means so much to me.

Because the conversations here have always been thoughtful, practical, and hopeful.

Especially now, when more Indian businesses are no longer asking:
“Do we need to care about ESG?”

They’re asking:
“How do we do this properly?”

That shift is important.

We still have a long way to go, but I genuinely believe more companies today want to build responsibly than we give them credit for.

Thank you to everyone who reads, shares, discusses, questions, or contributes here in any way.

10,000 is just a number.

But the people behind it make this space meaningful.

6d

【Interview Experience: Spotting Red Flags Before Signing the Offer】 Reflecting on a past interview experience from a few years ago that served as a great reminder of why "reverse interviewing" is so critical to preventing career mismatch. I was in the final round with a global tech company, involving stakeholders across multiple international time zones. Due to the significant time difference, the interview slots were set for either super early morning or late night. While handling off-hours calls is a common reality in global roles, the company insisted that I physically commute to their local office for the assessment, even though the overseas interviewers were comfortably joining via video call from their homes. Despite communicating my family constraints at the time (as a parent with a young child), they refused any flexibility or virtual options, citing "strict global policy". I requested to postpone the interview and ultimately decided to walk away from the process. My Takeaways: -The hiring process is a trailer for the actual job. If a company lacks empathy and flexibility during the honeymoon phase, they will likely expect you to sacrifice your personal life, health, and family time after you join. -Protect your non-negotiables. Sustainable high performance requires clear boundaries. No job or compensation is worth breaking your core values for. To TAs and Recruiters: - A huge shoutout to my agency partner back then, who fully backed my decision and negotiated fiercely on my behalf. Great products and compensation attract candidates, but Candidate Experience and mutual respect are what truly secure top talent. How do you evaluate cultural alignment during your interview process?#GlobalTech#CareerStrategy#CandidateExperience#WorkLifeBalance#JobSearch

I’ve spent nearly three decades in these markets, and I still remember the 2008 cycle with total clarity. Sitting in a client meeting, watching the FII sell figures flash across the terminal ~₹42,000 crore in a year. The room went silent. In those days, the logic was absolute: when foreign money left, the floor fell out. It wasn't about being a bear; it was just the structural reality of a "satellite" market. But as I look at the screen today, in 2026, I’m witnessing a completely different reality. The numbers are staggering. Foreign Portfolio Investors have pulled out ₹1.91 lakh crore in just the first four months of this year, more than the entire outflow of 2025. In March alone, we saw a record ₹1.26 lakh crore exit. In any other decade, that would have been a systemic collapse. Yet, the Nifty is range-bound. Because the domestic engine is firing with unprecedented force. Domestic Institutional Investors, including mutual funds, insurance companies, and the EPFO, invested ₹1.3 lakh crore during the first four months of the year, nearly mirroring FII inflows over the same period. Meanwhile, FPI ownership has quietly declined to a 15-year low of 14.7%, while domestic mutual fund (DII) ownership has climbed to a record 18.2% and continues to rise. So, who has the right thesis? The FII view is grounded in traditional fundamentals. India trades at a significant premium; earnings growth is moderating; and with oil at above USD 100/bl, the pressure on our current account and the rupee is very real. These aren't irrational fears; global capital is mobile and seeks the best risk-adjusted returns. The domestic thesis, however, is built on a different kind of conviction, one that is deeply personal. Think of the investor in Jaipur who puts aside ₹2,000 every month for an SIP. She isn't staring at a Bloomberg terminal or debating relative EM valuations. She is simply making a twenty-year bet on the country where she lives, works, and raises her children. To her, global volatility is just distant noise; her family’s future is the reality. She isn't just investing in a market, she is investing in her own life, and she isn't stopping for anyone. And this is the final decoupling. For the first time in our history, the Indian market has its own center of gravity. The FIIs are trading the 'India Premium' - they see a number that is too high. But the domestic investor is buying the 'India Century' - they see a future that is inevitable. One is a tactical trade; the other is a generational conviction. On Monday 27 April 2026, US service members at Naval Support Activity Bahrain began receiving WhatsApp messages on their personal phones. Signed Handala. The text:

"Your identities are fully known to our missile units. Soon you will be targeted by our Shahed drones and Kheibar missiles. We suggest you call your families now and say your final goodbyes."

The next day Handala — the cover identity for Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security, tracked as Storm-0842 — published the claimed personal details of 2,379 named US Marines. Rank. Unit. Home address. Family details. Daily commute. Shopping habits. Nightly leisure activities.

The security community's first instinct was to qualify the incident: the data was likely scraped from data brokers and social media rather than gathered from secure systems. That qualification reaches the opposite conclusion from the one intended.

If the targeting package for 2,379 named Marines was assembled from commercial sources rather than a breach, the threat is more serious, not less.

It means the intelligence collection system that produced personalised missile-threat messages required no exploit, no insider, no nation-state cyber capability, and no access to any classified system. It required a data broker account and a LinkedIn search.

This is the convergence article — the one that ties three previous DSI Chokepoint Doctrine pieces into a single argument:

→ The adtech surveillance piece: USCENTCOM confirmed targeting use of commercial location data, 14 April 2026.
→ The connected vehicle piece: the telemetry every modern car emits.
→ The Handala profile: who the actor is and what they do.

Three commercial data streams. One mosaic assembly. One personalised delivery channel — the most personal device in every Marine's pocket.

The adversary did not hack the military. It bought the data the military permitted its personnel to generate. That is the chokepoint no firewall closes.

If your organisation procures from any of the same data brokers — and most do — the same threat model applies to your executives, your board, and your operational personnel.

Whose name is in your supplier's catalogue this week?

Most people think a ₹600 restaurant meal is a better business than a ₹30 biscuit packet.

But structurally, businesses like Britannia and Nestlé often generate far higher returns with significantly lower capital intensity.

This is NOT truly an apple-to-apple comparison.

FMCG and restaurant businesses solve the same human need — food consumption — but through completely different economic models.

One scales through:
- distribution,
- repeat consumption,
- operating leverage,
- and brand habit.

The other scales through:
- physical expansion,
- service execution,
- customer experience,
- and location economics.

Britannia and Nestlé are already mature giants with limited growth runway.
Meanwhile, India’s QSR and restaurant industry may still be in the early innings of expansion.

The real question is:
Why do some business models structurally generate higher returns on capital than others?

Ces derniers jours sur LinkedIn, je vois de plus en plus de publications annonçant la “fin des ERP”.

Selon certains, avec l’IA, Claude Code, Lovable et les nouveaux outils de génération, il deviendrait bientôt inutile d’utiliser des ERP comme Divalto, Odoo, SAP ou Sage.

Honnêtement, je pense que la réalité est beaucoup plus nuancée.

Oui, l’IA va profondément transformer la manière de développer des logiciels.
Et c’est déjà en train de se produire.

Aujourd’hui, on peut :
➡️ développer beaucoup plus vite,
➡️ générer des interfaces en quelques minutes,
➡️ créer des workflows rapidement,
➡️ tester des idées plus facilement,
➡️ automatiser une partie du développement.

C’est une révolution technologique majeure.

Mais il y a une énorme différence entre :
👉 développer une petite application fonctionnelle,
et
👉 construire un ERP complet, robuste et capable de tenir pendant 10 ou 15 ans dans une entreprise.

Un ERP, ce n’est pas juste quelques écrans et une base de données.

C’est :

✔️ des dizaines d’années d’évolution,
✔️ des milliers de cas métiers gérés,
✔️ des contraintes réglementaires,
✔️ des problématiques de sécurité,
✔️ des enjeux de performance,
✔️ des mécanismes de traçabilité,
✔️ de la conformité légale,
✔️ des certifications,
✔️ des montées de version,
✔️ de la maintenance continue,
✔️ de l’interconnexion avec d’autres systèmes,
✔️ et surtout des milliers d’heures de retour terrain.

Développer seul une application avec l’IA n’a jamais été aussi accessible.
Et c’est une excellente chose.

Mais maintenir cette application dans le temps, la sécuriser, la faire évoluer, garantir sa stabilité, sa conformité et sa capacité à accompagner la croissance d’une entreprise… c’est une toute autre histoire.

Je pense que l’IA ne va pas remplacer les ERP.
En revanche, elle va profondément transformer la manière dont ils seront développés, personnalisés et intégrés.

Les éditeurs ERP qui sauront intégrer intelligemment l’IA dans leurs plateformes prendront probablement une énorme avance dans les prochaines années.

Et les intégrateurs ERP devront eux aussi évoluer :
✔️ moins de développement répétitif,
✔️ plus de conseil,
✔️ plus d’architecture,
✔️ plus d’accompagnement métier,
✔️ plus de vision globale des flux et des données.

L’IA va accélérer énormément de choses.
Mais construire un ERP fiable et durable restera encore longtemps un travail d’expérience, de méthode et de compréhension du terrain.

Et vous, pensez-vous que l’IA remplacera réellement les ERP historiques dans les prochaines années ? 👇

Ah, LinkedIn 🌈

All the scrolling of Instagram, but for people with lanyards.

Every second post seems to feature someone who is absolutely delighted to be attending a conference, thrilled to be moderating a panel, or honoured to be speaking at an event.

Maybe they are. Maybe I’ve been attending the wrong conferences all these years…  But if we’re honest, some of us are mostly delighted when the coffee is decent and we make it through the day without volunteering ourselves to sit on yet another steering group. 

This Pride Month, I’ve been thinking about authenticity.

Not corporate authenticity.
Not carefully curated content authenticity.
Not the kind that appears once a year when rainbow logos come out of storage.

You know… actual authenticity. 

The kind where people feel able to show up as themselves, admit when they don’t know something, and occasionally acknowledge that they are not, in fact, delighted by every aspect of professional life.

I’m generally not known for sitting quietly on the fence.

Sometimes that’s served me well.
Sometimes it’s got me into trouble.

But I’ve always believed leadership starts with being genuine. People don’t need polished perfection. They need honesty, integrity, and a reasonable chance that the person they’re talking to is the same person they’d meet over a coffee.

Rainbow logos have their place.

Visibility matters.
Representation matters.
Seeing organisations publicly support LGBT+ people matters.

But perhaps the challenge for all of us is moving from ‘rainbow washing’ visibility for profit to visibility for purpose.

Not asking, “How will this make us look?”

But asking, “How will this help people feel seen, valued and included?”

Belonging is what happens after the social media posts are written. It’s created through everyday conversations, leadership decisions, workplace cultures and communities where people feel able to show up as themselves without feeling the need to edit themselves to belong.

Not just during Pride Month. 
All year round, thanks. 🌈

🚀 Day 83/100 – LeetCode Daily Challenge

📌 Problem: 3753. Total Waviness of Numbers in Range II
🔗 https://lnkd.in/gSdC8Ugb

💡 Approach:
- The range can be extremely large, making brute-force enumeration impossible.
- Used Digit DP to count numbers and their total waviness efficiently.
- Process digits from left to right while maintaining:
 • Current position
 • Previous digits
 • Tight constraint (whether the prefix matches the limit)
 • Accumulated waviness count
- For each middle digit, determine whether it forms:
 • A peak (greater than both neighbors), or
 • A valley (smaller than both neighbors).
- Memoize DP states to avoid recomputation.
- Compute total waviness from 0 to num2 and subtract the result from 0 to num1−1.

✅ Time Complexity: O(D × States × 10)

✅ Space Complexity: O(States)

Yesterday, I crossed 10,000 followers on LinkedIn! 🥳

And somewhere along the way, this community became my favourite part of the internet.

10,000 people here now.

Honestly, that means a lot.

Because when I started posting on LinkedIn, I wasn’t trying to become a creator or build an audience.

I just wanted to make ESG and sustainability less overwhelming for businesses that genuinely want to do better, but don’t know where to begin.

And somewhere along the way, 10,000 people stayed for those conversations.

Founders.
ESG professionals.
Teams navigating GHG Accounting and BRSR for the first time.
People trying to understand how sustainability actually works beyond reports and buzzwords.

A few years ago, I probably looked at companies very differently.

During my Master’s in Environmental Economics, we were taught to see companies through a very critical lens, that growth and capitalism often come at the cost of people and the environment.

Then I started working with companies directly.

And my perspective changed.

Most companies are not intentionally trying to do harm.
Many are simply trying to balance business realities while figuring out what responsible growth should actually look like.

That belief became one of the foundations of PlanetaryPlus.

Not as a company that “calls out” businesses, but as someone who can work with them, guide them, and help them move from confusion to clarity. 

And honestly, that’s why this community means so much to me.

Because the conversations here have always been thoughtful, practical, and hopeful.

Especially now, when more Indian businesses are no longer asking:
“Do we need to care about ESG?”

They’re asking:
“How do we do this properly?”

That shift is important.

We still have a long way to go, but I genuinely believe more companies today want to build responsibly than we give them credit for.

Thank you to everyone who reads, shares, discusses, questions, or contributes here in any way.

10,000 is just a number.

But the people behind it make this space meaningful.

За 4 года я разобрал больше профилей, чем помню. На эфирах, в личных консультациях, с клиентами. И паттерн как правило всегда один: не одна ошибка, а 5:

🔹 Headline продаёт не ту роль или вообще не продаёт
🔹 Локация и Open to Work настроены против тебя, а не за
🔹 About написан “чтоб покороче”, а нужно наоборот
🔹 Рекомендаций нет или одна, а это бесплатное доверие
🔹 Стратегия размыта: “PM или продакт или аналитик - куда возьмут”. То есть никуда

Я устал повторять эти 5 вещей по сто раз. Поэтому собрал AI-агента, который говорит их за меня. Моим тоном, с конкретикой вместо «улучшите Headline». Агент обучен на дестяких моих видео и нескольких сотен тысяч строк текста.

Как это будет работать7?

Загружаешь PDF своего LinkedIn, агент смотрит на профиль глазами рекрутера + учитывает все последние тренды и алгоритмы Linkedin и выдаёт разбор: вердикт, что уже хорошо, а что нужно улучшить (5-8 конкретных правок, топ-3 приоритета) плюс скрытый потенциал.

Не “вам стоит лучше описать раздел About”, а «убери Project Manager, поставь Engineering Manager через слэш, смени локацию на Лондон, добавь нужные локации в Open to Work». То, что я сказал бы лично во время прожарки.

Открываю закрытую бету на 10 человек. Бесплатно. От вас взамен честная обратная связь: что попало, что нет, где тон промахнулся. 

Мне это нужно, чтобы решить, делать агента публичным или оставить в личном сопровождении.

Что нужно сделать. Просто напишите любой комментарий к посту и в течение дня выберу 10 человек, напишу в личку и мы вместе пройдемся по алгоритму

Поехали. 👇

P.S. Кто не попадёт в первую десятку, не страшно. Если эксперимент зайдёт, открою для всех, и подписчики канала получат доступ первыми. 😉

An “autonomous workforce” for independent agencies has made its way to GA (general availability) this week. While many teams may ask, "How fast can we pilot this?" the more critical question is, "How do we evaluate this correctly?" A new entrant is offering a solution that bundles AI agents with managed telephony, email deliverability, real-time ACORD quoting, and pre-built revenue workflows. In simple terms, these AI agents can handle phone calls and produce bound-ready ACORD 80 (Homeowners) or ACORD 90 (Auto) forms, integrating with major comparative raters. However, it's essential to focus on the following: 1) The unsexy layer matters most: - A2P registration - SHAKEN/STIR - CAN-SPAM - TCPA quiet hours - DNC scrubbing This compliance infrastructure is often overlooked by many “AI for agencies” tools. If not managed correctly, the entire operation can falter. 2) The real challenge lies downstream: - ACORD generation is relatively straightforward. - The complexities include: - Carrier appetite alignment - Rater integrations - Eligibility and underwriting feedback loops - Exception handling This is where automation can either succeed or fail. 3) Focus solely on core metrics: - If these metrics do not improve: - Bind rate - Quote-to-bind cycle time - Retention by producer - E&O exposure …then the solution is not adding value. In my view, this category is legitimate. By 2027, agencies lacking an AI foundation may find themselves at a competitive disadvantage regarding producer capacity. However, it’s crucial to remember that a vendor demo does not equate to a successful deployment, and “autonomous” does not mean it meets product specifications. One important nuance: ACORD 80/90 ≠ guaranteed carrier acceptance. They standardize intake — not underwriting. Carrier appetite, state rules, and eligibility still determine whether a risk actually binds. That gap is where most “AI” claims get tested.#insuretech#ai#aiininsurance#pandcdistribution

Takayuki Kinoshita

Takayuki Kinoshita (木下 隆之, Kinoshita Takayuki) is a Japanese racing car driver, author, and automotive journalist. Kinoshita is affiliated with Toyota Motorsport's GAZOO Racing arm, with whom he scored SP8 class wins in the 2010, 2012, and 2014 24 Hours Nürburgring driving the Lexus LFA. He also won A8 class in the 2004 24 Hours Nürburgring driving a Nissan Skyline GT-R(R34) for Falken Motorsports.

Among Japanese drivers, Kinoshita has raced the most times in the 24 Hours Nürburgring. He has also raced in All Japan Grand Touring Car Championship, Japanese Touring Car Championship, Japanese Formula Three, and Super Taikyu N1 Endurance Series.

Kinoshita is a member of the Automotive Journalists Association of Japan and is on the selection committee for Car of the Year Japan. He was also a presenter on the Japanese Best Motoring TV series.

Obscure Japanese Film #248

| Toru Shimamura |
| --- |

This Nikkatsu production was based on the autobiographical novel of the same name by one of Japan’s major writers, Yasushi Inoue (1907-91). The book was translated into English by Jean Oda Moy in 1991, but Inoue’s sequel, Zoku Shirobamba, has been neither filmed nor translated, and the fact that Nikkatsu never made the sequel suggests that this film was not especially profitable. The story concerns Inoue’s own childhood in Izu in the early Taisho period (1912-26) when Inoue was around seven years old, and the title refers to the white aphids that the children would try to catch in the autumn.

| Izumi Ashikawa |
| --- |

Inoue’s alter ego is Kosaku (played here by Toru [later Miki] Shimamura), whose rural upbringing is unusual in that his parents, though living, are absent, and he’s brought up by his late great-great uncle’s mistress, known as Granny Onui (Tanie Kitabayashi). He’s all she’s got, so she spoils him, and he’s very attached to her as a result. The only other person he really likes is Sakiko (Izumi Ashikawa), whom he calls his elder sister although she’s actually his aunt. Unfortunately, she looks down on Onui and there’s no love lost between the two women. Sakiko lives in the ‘Upper House’ nearby with Kosaku’s other relations, but he feels uncomfortable there and avoids them. Kosaku gets the highest grades in his year at school and his family has a higher social status than his classmates’, so he feels different to the other boys and great things are expected of him.

| Jacket of the novel in English translation |
| --- |

Reading the novel in translation a while ago I was reminded of the films of Keisuke Kinoshita and wondered if the book had ever been filmed; looking it up, I found that not only had it been, but that the screenwriter was none other than Keisuke Kinoshita himself. However, it’s directed not by him, but by Eisuke Takizawa, who seems to have been Nikkatsu’s director of choice for their more prestigious literary adaptations during this period (not a genre they’re widely remembered for).

| Jukichi Uno |

เคสุเกะ คิโนชิตะ ชีวประวัติและผลงานภาพยนตร์

---

เคสุเกะ คิโนชิตะ(木下 惠介, Kinoshita Keisuke ; 5 ธันวาคม 1912 – 30 ธันวาคม 1998)เป็นผู้กำกับภาพยนตร์และนักเขียนบทภาพยนตร์ชาวญี่ปุ่น [2]แม้ว่าจะเป็นที่รู้จักในระดับนานาชาติน้อยกว่านักแสดงร่วมสมัยอย่างอากิระ คุโรซาวะเคนจิ มิโซกุจิและยาสุจิโร โอซุแต่เขาก็เป็นบุคคลสำคัญในครัวเรือนของประเทศบ้านเกิด เป็นที่รักของทั้งนักวิจารณ์และผู้ชมตั้งแต่ทศวรรษที่ 1940 ถึง 1960 ภาพยนตร์ของคิโนชิตะโดดเด่นด้วยความรู้สึกซาบซึ้ง ความบริสุทธิ์ และความงาม และมักมีการทดลองทั้งด้านเทคนิคและเนื้อหา

คิโนชิตะเข้าสู่วงการภาพยนตร์ในปี 1933 ในฐานะผู้ประมวลผลฟิล์ม เขาได้เลื่อนตำแหน่งเป็นผู้ช่วยกล้อง จากนั้นจึงย้ายไปเป็นผู้ช่วยผู้กำกับ ในปี 1943 คิโนชิตะได้รับการเลื่อนตำแหน่งเป็นผู้กำกับและได้ออกฉายภาพยนตร์เรื่องแรกของเขาเรื่องPort of Flowersคิโนชิตะเป็นผู้กำกับภาพยนตร์ที่มีผลงานมากมาย เขาได้กำกับภาพยนตร์ 43 เรื่องในช่วง 23 ปีแรกของอาชีพการงาน และอีก 5 เรื่องหลังจากทำงานด้านการผลิตรายการโทรทัศน์ ภาพยนตร์ที่เป็นที่รู้จักมากที่สุดของเขา ได้แก่ Carmen Comes Home(1951), A Japanese Tragedy(1953), Twenty-Four Eyes(1954), She Was Like a Wild Chrysanthemum(1955) และ The Ballad of Narayama(1958)

## ชีวประวัติ

### ช่วงแรกๆ (พ.ศ. 2455–2486)

เคสุเกะ คิโน ชิตะ เกิดเมื่อวันที่ 5 ธันวาคม ค.ศ. 1912 ที่เมืองฮามามัตสึ จังหวัดชิซุโอกะเป็นบุตรคนที่สี่จากบุตรแปดคนของพ่อค้า ชูกิจิ คิโนชิตะ และภรรยาของเขา ทามะ ครอบครัวของเขาผลิตผักดองและเป็นเจ้าของร้านขายของชำ[1]เขาเป็นแฟนภาพยนตร์ตั้งแต่ยังเด็ก และให้คำมั่นสัญญาว่าจะเป็นผู้สร้างภาพยนตร์ แต่ต้องเผชิญกับการต่อต้านจากพ่อแม่[3]ดังนั้นเขาจึงเข้าเรียนมัธยมปลายและเริ่มเรียนต่อในระดับวิทยาลัย[3]

วันหนึ่ง ขณะที่คิโนชิตะยังเรียนอยู่ชั้นมัธยมปลาย ทีมงานภาพยนตร์ได้เดินทางมาถึงฮามามัตสึเพื่อถ่ายทำนอกสถานที่[3]หนึ่งในทีมงานมีนักแสดงจูโนะสุเกะ บันโด ซึ่งคิโนชิตะจะเป็นเพื่อนกับเขาเมื่อบันโดมาที่ร้านขายของชำของครอบครัวคิโนชิตะ[3]บันโดช่วยคิโนชิตะหนีไปเกียวโตซึ่งเป็นที่ที่ภาพยนตร์ย้อนยุคส่วนใหญ่ถ่ายทำ แต่ปู่ของคิโนชิตะมาและพาคิโนชิตะกลับบ้านในวันรุ่งขึ้น[3]ความมุ่งมั่นของคิโนชิตะที่จะเป็นผู้สร้างภาพยนตร์ทำให้พ่อแม่ของเขาตัดสินใจให้เขามีอาชีพในวงการภาพยนตร์[3]

แม่ของคิโนชิตะได้แนะนำให้เขารู้จักกับสตูดิโอ Shochiku Kamataซึ่งยาสุจิโร โอซุและมิกิโอะ นารุเสะทำงานอยู่[3] [4]แต่คิโนชิตะได้รับแจ้งว่าเขาไม่สามารถเป็นผู้ช่วยผู้กำกับได้หากไม่มีการศึกษาระดับมหาวิทยาลัย แต่เขาอาจสามารถเป็นช่างภาพได้[3]เขาสมัครเข้าเรียนที่โรงเรียนถ่ายภาพตะวันออก แต่ได้รับแจ้งว่าเขาต้องมีประสบการณ์จริงอย่างน้อยครึ่งปีจึงจะเข้าเรียนได้[3]จากนั้นเขาทำงานในร้านถ่ายภาพในโตเกียวจนกระทั่งเขามีประสบการณ์เพียงพอที่จะสมัครเข้าเรียนที่โรงเรียนถ่ายภาพตะวันออก[3]เขาสำเร็จการศึกษา จากนั้นได้รับการตอบรับเข้าเรียนที่ Shochiku ในปี 1933 แต่ได้รับแจ้งว่าพวกเขาไม่ต้องการผู้ช่วยกล้องอีกต่อไปและเขาจะต้องทำงานในห้องปฏิบัติการประมวลผลฟิล์ม[3]จากนั้นคิโนชิตะจึงย้ายไปทำงานเป็นผู้ช่วยกล้องภายใต้การดูแลของยาสุจิโร ชิมาซึ [ 3]หลังจากนั้นสองปี ชิมาซึได้ขอให้หัวหน้าของคิโนชิตะย้ายคิโนชิตะไปดำรงตำแหน่งผู้ช่วยผู้กำกับ แต่คำขอถูกปฏิเสธ[3]หลังจากนั้นอีกหนึ่งปี Shimazu เองก็ได้แต่งตั้ง Kinoshita ให้เป็นผู้ช่วยผู้กำกับของเขา[3] Kinoshita ให้เครดิต Shimazu ในฐานะที่ปรึกษาที่สำคัญที่สุดข

> — 猿渡 哲也 (@4B3lPouP3615880) February 24, 2025

猿渡哲也氏は『高校鉄拳伝タフ』、『TOUGH-タフ-』などシリーズ作をヒットさせ、現在は『TOUGH 龍を継ぐ男』を連載中。シリーズ累計発行部数は1000万部を突破している。 『高校鉄拳伝タフ』や『TOUGH-タフ-』の主人公である宮沢熹一（キー坊）は、当初はお調子者だが、格闘家としてさまざまな死線をくぐり抜ける中で次第に成長を遂げていく。 迫力ある作画で描かれる格闘シーンは読者に強いインパクトをもたらし、また台詞もあわせたそのキャッチーさはたびたび読者のあいだで話題になる。キー坊の「ウ…ウソやろ こ…こんなことが こんなことが許されていいのか」の1コマを知っている人は多いことだろう。

## 2026年5月最新！X（旧Twitter）の不具合を徹底深掘り【Part 1：今まさに起きている現実】

今日はX（旧Twitter）を使っていて「またか…」とため息をついた経験がある方へ向けて、2026年5月15日現在の不具合状況をしっかり整理してお伝えします。私自身も朝から返信が送れず、タイムラインが古い投稿ばかり流れてきてイライラした一人です。

ただの愚痴ではなく、ユーザーとして役立つ情報にまとめました。この記事は全5パートのシリーズです。Part 1では「今起きている現実」に焦点を当てます。最後まで読んでいただければ、状況が整理されて「なるほど」と思えるはずです。

### 今日（2026年5月15日）のリアルな状況

Downdetectorなどの障害報告サイトを確認しても、大規模な完全ダウンは起きていません。しかし、過去24時間以内の報告では「アプリ関連38%」「投稿/返信34%」「ログイン14%」が目立っています。

日本ユーザーからも以下のような声が相次いでいます。

- 返信が見えない・送信できない
- 引用ポストもエラーになる
- ミュートしたアカウントの投稿が流れてくる
- DM通知の遅延

昨日から症状が続いている人も少なくありません。Twitter時代は「稀に起きるダウン」だったのが、今は「日常的に微妙に使いづらい」状態が続いている印象です。

### 2026年全体の不具合傾向まとめ

今年に入ってから1〜4月だけでも複数回の大規模障害が発生しました。主な症状は以下の通りです。

| 症状カテゴリ | 詳細 | 発生頻度 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 投稿・返信関連 | 「送信できません」で止まる、下書きに残る | 非常に高い |
| タイムライン異常 | 最新反映されない、2分問題の再発 | 高い |
| アプリ挙動不良 | 新Androidアプリ移行後の不具合 | 中〜高 |
| DM・通知 | 遅延や表示バグ | 中 |

この表からもわかるように、特に投稿・返信関連のトラブルが日常化しています。私も含め、多くのユーザーが「最近振り回されっぱなし」と感じているようです。

### 誰が一番困っているのか

特に影響を受けやすいのは以下の層です。

- 配信者・クリエイター（返信遅れでエンゲージメント低下）
- リアルタイム情報を追う人
- ビジネスユーザー
- 日本ユーザー（Xを日常会話ツールとして使っている層が多い）

ちょっとした不具合でもストレスが溜まりやすい環境です。

Part 2では「本質的な原因とこれからの展望」について深掘りします。引き続きお付き合いいただけると嬉しいです。

## 2026年5月最新！X（旧Twitter）の不具合を徹底深掘り【Part 2：本質的な原因と解決策】

Part 1では、2026年5月15日現在のX（旧Twitter）のリアルな不具合状況をお伝えしました。今回は「なぜこんなに頻繁に不具合が起きるのか」という本質的な原因と、私が実際に効果的だと感じている解決策をまとめます。

### X不具合の根本原因とは

原因はシンプルです。「Everything App化を急ぎすぎている」点にあります。

XはもはやただのSNSではなく、決済機能（X Money）、Grok AI統合、カスタムタイムライン、XChatなど、複数の大型機能を同時に推進しています。バックエンドへの負荷が非常に大きく、昔のスタッフ削減の影響もまだ残っています。

機能追加のスピードが安定性を上回っている状態が続いているため、Twitter時代のように「稀にダウン」ではなく、「日常的に微妙に使いづらい」状況を生み出しています。

### 2026年現在、主な原因と影響度

| 主な原因 | 詳細 | 影響度 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Everything App化の加速 | X Money、Grok統合、動画・長文機能などの同時開発 | ★★★★☆ |
| サーバー・インフラ負荷 | ユーザー増加＋新機能によるバックエンド圧迫 | ★★★★★ |
| アプリ更新の頻度 | 新Androidアプリ移行後の不安定化 | ★★★☆☆ |
| 人員・運用体制 | 過去の大幅スタッフ削減の影響 | ★★★☆☆ |

この表を見ると、特にサーバー負荷と新機能開発のバランスが最大の課題であることがわかります。

### 今すぐ試せる実践的な解決策

私が日常的に使っていて効果が高い順に並べました。

1. ブラウザ版（PC）を併用する – アプリより明らかに安定しています
2. アプリのキャッシュクリア or 再インストール – 特にAndroidユーザーは効果大
3. 不具合発生時は「一旦待つ」 – 多くの場合、数時間〜半日以内に回復
4. Grokに聞く – 「今のX不具合状況教えて」と聞くと最新情報を教えてくれます
5. 通知オフ→オン切り替えや、機内モードON/OFFでリフレッシュ

これらを実践するだけで、かなりストレスが減ります。私もこの組み合わせでかなり快適に使えるようになりました。

ただし根本解決はX社側での改善が必要です。成長痛の時期ではありますが、ユーザー体験を犠牲にしすぎると、せっかくの新機能（X Moneyなど）も「またバグるのでは…」と信用されにくくなってしまいます。

Part 3では「クリエイター・ビジネスユーザー向けの影響と対策」に焦点を当てます。引き続き読んでいただけると嬉しいです。

A small cultural note that makes a big difference

In working with colleagues in Japan, one small detail can go a long way: the use of “-san.” Using “-san” isn’t just a linguistic habit — it’s a simple expression of respect, professionalism, and equality. While it’s perfectly fine to call someone by their first name without “-san,” using a last name without any honorific (for example, calling someone just “Yamada”) can come across as disrespectful.

From my own experience, being addressed by last name only usually happened in very specific contexts — school, among close friends, or in highly hierarchical environments. Even then, I personally avoided addressing others that way.

If someone calls me “Sugita (my last name)” without an honorific, I usually ask them to use “Kats (my first name)” or “Sugita‑san,” regardless of our relationship. Not because of formality — but because respect matters, and it’s often conveyed through small, thoughtful actions.

Being mindful of these nuances helps build trust and makes cross‑cultural collaboration smoother for everyone.

Like everyone else, I also have good days and bad days. Running is my best way to refresh my mind. During a run today, an idea suddenly came back to me: Yoshuku.

A few years ago, a professional Yoshuku practitioner was invited to our Tokyo headquarters, and around 30–40 people joined the session. I was one of them. At that time, I didn’t fully realize how deeply this concept connects with both our culture and modern business thinking. Yoshuku is a Japanese tradition of celebrating success in advance. Originally linked to prayers for a good harvest, it can be seen today as a form of success-oriented mental simulation. 

If we constantly imagine failure, our actions often follow that direction. But when we create concrete and detailed images of success, we begin to see what really matters—key actions, potential pitfalls, and risks we should avoid.

Inspired by this, I’ve decided to restart a personal Yoshuku routine every Monday—a moment to clearly and positively visualize success before it happens. I’m curious to see how this mindset will influence my thinking and actions over time, and I hope to share some good progress with you in the future.

予祝で「人財の可能性」を解き放つ：成功を先に描く習慣 

誰にでもそうだと思いますが、私にも良い日もあれば、そうでない日もあります。私にとって一番のリフレッシュはランニングです。今日走っている途中で、ふと 「予祝」 という言葉が頭に浮かびました。

数年前、予祝のプロフェッショナルの方を東京本社にお招きし、30〜40名ほどでセッションを行ったことがありました。私もその一人でした。当時は、この考え方が日本の文化だけでなく、現代のビジネスにも深くつながっていることを、今ほど実感していなかったように思います。予祝とは、「成功を先に祝う」日本の伝統です。もともとは豊作祈願のような祈りの行為ですが、現代的に言えば 成功を前提としたメンタル・シミュレーション と捉えることもできます。

失敗のイメージばかりを持っていると、行動も自然とその方向に引き寄せられてしまいます。一方で、成功した状態を具体的かつ鮮明に思い描くことで、本当に大切な行動や、避けるべき落とし穴、リスクが見えてきます。

そんなことを考えながら、毎週月曜日に予祝の習慣を再開する ことにしました。起こる前に、前向きに、成功をしっかりイメージする時間です。このマインドセットがこれからの思考や行動にどんな影響を与えるのか、自分自身でも楽しみにしています。いずれ、良い進捗をご報告できればと思います。

In Japan, the traditional way of paying respect at a shrine—two bows, two claps, one bow—carries profound meaning. This ritual is more than a series of gestures:
• Bow twice: a moment to show respect and humility.
• Clap twice: a way to open your heart and express sincerity.
• Bow once again: a gesture of gratitude and closure.
This rhythm reminds me of the mindset we value in business: beginning with respect for others, showing sincerity through action, and ending with gratitude, which strengthens relationships and trust.
 
Perhaps you have your own rituals that bring clarity to your new year. I would love to hear how you greet the new year or what traditions inspire you as you set your goals for 2026.

Ekiden: A Lesson in Shared Purpose, Resilience—and Grace in Defeat

Every January, millions in Japan tune in to watch the Hakone Ekiden, a two-day, 217 km (135 mile) university relay race. It’s more than a sporting event—it’s a living example of leadership, teamwork, and character. The word Ekiden means “station to station,” rooted in an ancient courier system. Today, the sash (tasuki) symbolizes trust, responsibility, and continuity. Each runner pushes beyond personal limits, not for individual glory, but to honor the team and the shared goal. 

Sometimes, we witness something even more inspiring: grace in defeat.
I’ll never forget a team captain who gave a heartfelt speech after his team—expected to win after dominating two prior races—fell short. He thanked his general managers and teammates, made humble reflection of the race and then shouted, “I love my team!” despite the loss. Finally, he promised that his successors would win next year.
Moments like these remind us:
• We cannot always enjoy great business outcomes.
• Being a good loser—and learning from setbacks—is just as important as winning.
He embodied that spirit.

Ekiden is true teamwork:
• Success is a relay of effort, trust, and adaptability.
• Passing the baton—knowledge, responsibility, encouragement—is as critical as running your leg.
• Leadership means creating conditions where every runner feels their role is vital.

Every year, I cheer the runners in person. It’s my New Year ritual, and their determination gives me incredible energy. If you’re in Japan, I highly recommend experiencing it in person—or at least watching it on TV. You’ll gain a deeper understanding of Japanese culture and its emphasis on collective purpose: valuing the team over the individual, prioritizing endurance over speed, and cherishing the act of “passing on” responsibility. These principles are deeply woven into how Japanese organizations operate.

As we start a new year, let’s ask ourselves: “How can we design our teams to run like an Ekiden—aligned, resilient, and inspired by a common purpose?”

Great slides aren’t decoration—they’re strategy.

Too often we see the same deck used for a team update, an executive decision meeting, and a broad town hall. The result? Dense slides, tiny fonts, and audiences who can’t engage.

For me, slide design is both Inclusion and Business Effectiveness:
• Inclusion: Design for everyone in the room (and on the call). Use clear hierarchy, large readable fonts, high contrast, minimal jargon, and one message per slide. If people can’t read it, they can’t contribute.
• Plain Language for Global Audiences: Global leaders avoid overly sophisticated word choices because many listeners are non‑native English speakers. I appreciate that almost all Astellas senior leaders are mindful of this and consistently communicate so everyone can follow and contribute.
• Business Effectiveness: Tailor to the occasion. Executives need a crisp story and a clear “ask.” Broad communications need simplicity and clarity. Fewer, sharper slides improve decision velocity and alignment.

As leaders, our responsibility is to communicate accessibly and decide decisively. Let’s choose readability over density and clarity over completeness—and get better outcomes for our people and our business.

Inclusion at Astellas: business discipline that creates VALUE for patients
Inclusion at Astellas isn’t a slogan—it’s the way we turn innovative science into real‑world outcomes for patients. When we all stay relentlessly business‑oriented, inclusion becomes practical and measurable: we learn what the business needs, and we co‑create solutions that move the business.
To keep that discipline, our meetings run on a one‑page proposal. On a single page we capture:
• Topic
• Why now (why this deserves the meeting)
• Options (viable solutions)
• Today’s recommendation & why
• Timeline
• Cost proposal
Charts or a table can be attached, but only the one‑pager is presented on the day—because clarity invites diverse voices, focuses debate on decisions, and accelerates execution. At Astellas, if a proposal is not presented as a one‑pager, it will not be tabled for discussion or approval.
Inclusion is also imagination. It asks: What do they need? How can I support them? Without imagination, we cannot work well in any organization. Imagination helps us anticipate needs, design better options, and include perspectives that might otherwise be missed.
From my experience as CPO at Astellas, initiatives go well when we follow this guideline. When we don’t, even high‑quality proposals face challenges. The difference is business‑side buy‑in and understanding the audience—without those, HR initiatives risk becoming self‑satisfaction rather than business impact.
HR experts often default to technical explanations, but what the business truly needs is a clear line of sight to how the proposal drives our business—pipeline impact, operational efficiency, and patient outcomes. HR is part of the business, not adjacent to it. Thinking from that point of view is critical.
When we combine diverse perspectives with business rigor, we make faster, smarter decisions—and that’s how we win for patients and for Astellas.

Impact-Focused: Prioritizing What Truly Matters
Many people find it essential to prioritize and focus on what really matters. As Kobe Bryant once said that he had given full priority to everything he could do to become the best basketball player. Then how about another way to say this? "If you were to die tomorrow or next week, what would you like to accomplish today or this week?" "How do I really want to spend my day today?" That's the question. It means that we should put our effort into believing that it really matters, rather than reacting to feeling urgent. Our lives are shorter than we think. 
In professional life, it's easy to get caught up in tasks that need to be addressed immediately, and it's easy to neglect long-term goals that are important but not urgent. Many people tend to focus their energy on important and urgent things, and then turn to unimportant but urgent things. It is quite difficult to pay proper attention to important matters that do not require immediate action if you are not aware of it. 
To be honest, I'm good at troubleshooting and day-to-day problem-solving, but I'm not very good at strategic thinking. This is because in my career, I have prioritized urgent and less important tasks for my internal clients. My advice to the next generation is to focus enough on strategic priorities rather than focusing too much on the wants of our internal and external customers. If we want to accomplish something important, we should not seek recognition or admiration from others.

Active recovery - Japanese follows English
 
I hope you're all doing well. I wanted to share an interesting concept that's been beneficial for me: active recovery. It comes from the sports world, where it's understood that complete rest after intense activity (such as long distance races) isn't always the best approach. We all have busy lives, and it's common to hear people say they need to sleep all day on weekends. Even if I want to sleep in on Saturday, my dog wakes me up at 5 AM, just like any other day.

I can go for a long-distance run, catch up on reading, and spend quality time with my wife discussing various topics. This sense of accomplishment and the extra energy it brings is quite rewarding.
Engaging in active recovery not only refreshes me but also promotes better balance. Exercise allows my brain to take a break and my muscles to release tension, leading to a more refreshed and balanced state. I hope you find this concept as beneficial as I do. Have a great day ahead!

Additionally, participating in a short-term assignment can pave the way for long-term assignments if needed later.

How to get control of our time

I recently came across a message that resonated with me, and I wanted to share it with all of you as I believe it could significantly enhance our workflow and communication. The message stated: "If I do not receive any response from you prior to [specified deadline], I will assume you have no edits to this latest draft, and I will proceed."
 
I think this approach is fantastic for maintaining a sense of urgency and ensuring that projects move forward without unnecessary delays. It is both polite and effective, and it fosters accountability. By not responding, you are essentially signaling trust and delegation, which can be very empowering.
 
Many years ago, I had the experience of working with a great supervisor who was in a different country. Despite their many strengths, their response speed was a weak point that often slowed down my work. This situation led to frustration and a realization that I needed a better way to manage communication. My mentor recommended the same proactive communication technique “if I don’t receive…”, and it dramatically changed my professional life.
 
By using this approach, I was able to control my work and plan my timing more effectively. It required me to be outcome-focused and accountable for the results, but it also provided a sense of empowerment and control over my schedule. I highly recommend this method to all of you. It allows you to plan your actions and manage your timing independently, leading to improved efficiency and productivity. It will increase your white space, definitely.

Let’s Break the Silence Around Menopause at Work

For too long, menopause has been treated as a private issue, when it is clearly a workplace one too. Our global Menopause Experience and Attitudes Study, covering 13,800 respondents across six countries, shows just how widespread the impact is:
- Over a third of people going through menopause experience some kind of negative impact at work.
- 1 in 20 believe they’ve lost out on promotions or pay rises.
- Many feel unable to talk to colleagues or managers.

This is a reality we can and must change.

That’s why I’m proud to support Astellas’ Pledge to Champion a Menopause-Inclusive Workplace. Through education, training, and open dialogue, we aim to create a culture where no one feels they have to suffer in silence.

This is about health, inclusion, and respect.

It’s also a reminder that leadership means listening, even when the topic is uncomfortable. It is especially important we listen then.

As I mentioned the other day, business leadership is essential for the realization of HR measures. In this article, I would like to introduce specific success stories.

A recent conversation with people from the media gave me a chance to reflect on the evolving role of HR and the essence of human capital management.

Why do we need an HR department in the first place? My time at a global company challenged my assumptions more than any other experience. Before joining, I led HR for a Japanese subsidiary, where I naturally took the lead in talent and organizational discussions during regional and HQ reviews. It felt like a clear part of HR’s job. But at the company, the expectation was different. HR’s role was to coach and prepare business leaders—both regional / HQ and local—so they could lead meaningful conversations about talent and organization themselves.　At first, I thought, “It would be faster and more effective if I just did it myself.” But I soon realized: this is the point.

Talent and organizational matters are as fundamental to business as finance. As global leaders often say, “Finance in one hand, HR in the other.” Strong leaders take ownership of hiring, development, rewards, and culture. They don’t delegate these decisions and accountabilities entirely to HR—they shape them as part of their business strategy.

It may take more effort upfront, but unless business leaders truly own their talent and organizational challenges, HR initiatives risk being seen as disconnected or “just another program.” This isn’t about HR simply following business. It’s about HR identifying challenges, proposing solutions, and guiding leaders until they feel the challenge is their own.

I’d love to hear your thoughts. How is HR evolving in your organization?

最近のメディアとの会話は、人事の役割の進化と人的資本管理の本質について考える機会を与えてくれました。

そもそもなぜ人事部門が必要なのでしょうか?グローバル企業で過ごした時間は、他のどの経験よりも私の思い込みに挑戦しました。そちらへの入社前は日本法人の人事を率いていましたが、リージョンや本社のレビューでは、自然と人材や組織の議論を私が主導していました。それは人事部の仕事の明確な一部のように感じていました。しかし、その企業では人事への期待が私の想定とは違っていました。人事部の役割は、リージョン・本社と各国の両方のビジネスリーダーをコーチし、準備することで、人材と組織について有意義な会話を彼らが自分で主導できるようにすることでした。最初は「自分でやった方が早く、効果的だ」と思っていました。しかし、私はすぐに、これが重要ポイントであることに気づきました。

人材と組織の問題は、財務と同じくらいビジネスにとって基本的なものです。グローバルリーダーがよく言うように、「片手には財務、もう片方には人事」。強力なリーダーは、採用、能力開発、報酬、文化に責任を持ちます。これらの決定と説明責任を完全に人事部に委任するのではなく、ビジネス戦略の一部として形成します。

事前により多くの労力が必要になるかもしれませんが、ビジネスリーダーが自分のタレントと組織の課題を真に認識しない限り、人事イニシアチブはビジネスから分断された、または「単なる別のプログラム」と見なされるリスクがあります。ここで言いたいことは、人事部が単にビジネスをフォローするだけではありません。それは、人事部が課題を特定し、解決策を提案し、課題が自分のものであると感じるまでリーダーを導くことです。

I recently came across some fantastic insights on the importance of asking questions, particularly from Michael Marquardt and Bob Tiede's work – Leading with Questions. It reminded me of a tech giant CEO who always encouraged employees to ask questions, demonstrating an incredibly strong growth mindset. This practice has made me realize that asking questions is a key behavior that I often forget. I tend to jump straight to answers or recommendations, which isn't always the best approach.

Many exceptional leaders talk less and ask more questions, guiding their teams in the right direction. Even asking seemingly "stupid" questions can be beneficial, as it fosters a sense of psychological safety within the team. When leaders ask questions, it shows that it's okay for others to do the same. This approach is particularly useful when dealing with topics we're not entirely familiar with, as it allows us to delegate tasks more effectively.

It's essential to remember that asking questions shouldn't come across as accusatory. Instead, it requires good listening skills and can help resolve conflicts. Confident leaders aren't afraid to ask questions, as they understand that it doesn't make them appear weak. Some valuable questions to ask include: "How can I help you?", "What do you need to make it even better or quicker?", "What could we have done better?", "What would you do if you had the chance again?", "If we don't do this, what will happen?", and "What can be the best and worst-case scenarios?".

Ultimately, everything ties back to having a growth mindset for the future. I'm eager to continue improving my questioning skills and would love to hear your thoughts on this topic.

To change our culture, we take down walls…literally.
 
At Astellas, we’ve been working hard to evolve our culture. Not just in what we say, but in how we lead, decide, and work together. Last month, we took a visible step forward: the top floor of our Tokyo HQ, once home to executive offices and the formal meeting space known as the “Decision Room,” has been fully transformed. No more private suites. No more separate executive floor.
 
In its place, we opened the One Astellas Floor, an open-plan space where senior leaders and employees now sit and collaborate side-by-side. Half of the floor is open plan, hot-desk seating for all colleagues, just like any other part of the office. This wasn’t just a renovation; it was a deliberate choice.
 
By stepping away from the Executive Floor and retiring the formal Decision Room, we’re moving beyond outdated symbols of hierarchy that can distance leaders from teams. In their place, we’re creating open spaces—both physically and culturally—where every colleague feels confident to speak up, share ideas, and shape our future together.
 
This change reflects the culture we’re building—flatter, more transparent, and more connected. It’s a reminder that leadership isn’t defined by square footage or seating charts, but by how accessible we are to the people we lead.
 
Sometimes, changing a culture starts by changing the floorplan!

The world of work is complex, exciting, and moving at a pace I’ve never seen before. And yet, the principle guiding our decisions every day is simple: if what we’re doing isn’t accelerating the business and helping teams do their best work, we should pause and ask why we’re doing it at all. 
 
Here’s what I know to be true as I step into year two: 
 
Clarity beats complexity. Talking to each other like humans in simple, plain language unlocks speed, understanding, and trust. 
 
Build with, not just for. Pressure‑test assumptions and stay customer‑obsessed, especially when the customer is our employees. Now more than ever, we have to stay close to the business, pay attention to what’s working (and what isn’t), and adjust quickly.  
 
Unlearning matters just as much as learning. Too often, holding onto what once worked slows down progress. When we’re willing to let go of what was, we expand what’s possible. We create space for better ideas, faster decisions, and stronger outcomes. 
 
To every person I've had the chance to connect with this year — our employees across the globe, my peers, our customers — thank you. You are the reason this work is worth doing and I’m honored to work alongside you. Here's to year two!

Rahul Jindal's latest paper on “Organizational Metabolism” is a masterclass in shifting our focus from AI adoption to AI absorption. His core thesis? The real differentiator in 2026 isn't your technology budget—it’s your "Metabolic Rate."
The framework’s biggest win is the concept of Workflow Debt. We are often layering AI on top of legacy processes instead of retiring them. As Rahul puts it: "Low-metabolism organizations accumulate experiments. High-metabolism organizations retire workflows."
The one piece I think we still need to solve for: The Emotional Metabolism.
While the structural roadmap is brilliant, we can’t ignore the "human immune system." Retiring a workflow can feel like retiring an identity. For an organization to truly become "Adaptive," we have to figure out how to build the psychological safety that allows teams to dismantle their own processes without fearing for their future.

The agentic enterprise is here! 🚀

This guy sells diesel trucks by hip thrusting at the camera… he’s hip thrusting at the trucks, too. people LOVE it. Hundreds of thousands of views. Massive engagement. People in the comments are literally asking where they can buy trucks. Even crazier? Another creator copied the exact format for water tankers… and went from barely getting views to pulling 400K+ views in days. Why does this work? I call it The Law of Total Commitment The internet rewards conviction. Especially when someone is fully committed to the bit. ⸻ Jerry’s videos work because he’s all in. No corporate polish. No trying to look “professional.” No holding back. Just total commitment. The outfits. The dancing. The energy. The absurdity. You believe HE believes. And that level of conviction becomes magnetic. ⸻ People watch not because they suddenly care about diesel truck specs… but because committed energy feels alive. Now, most brands shouldn’t copy the exact format. If GLAMNETIC suddenly started hip thrusting at press-on nails… that would probably hurt the brand. 😂 But brands SHOULD study the principle underneath it: Don’t copy the expression. Copy the commitment level. Because total commitment only works when it aligns with the brand’s identity. So what would “total commitment” look like for our brands? EagleRidge Roofing and Construction We already lean heavily into Lance as the Local Legend. But what if we went even further? Lance’s 8 kids becoming part of the “crew.” Funny roofing songs and dances. Ridiculous family skits about what makes a great roof. Ridge the eagle making random appearances like some patriotic mascot. 😂 Not random absurdity. A deeper commitment to the personality and world we’re already building. ⸻ GLAMNETIC We already heavily leverage Ann because honestly… she’s the unicorn. But we could commit even harder to the world-building side of the brand. Ann choosing Met Gala gowns AND matching nails. Full transformation rituals. More cinematic beauty storytelling. Building out an even bigger Glamnetic universe around beauty, fantasy, confidence, and identity. Quitine We already embrace the real human side of quitting. But what if we leaned even harder into helping people replace destructive addictions with healthy new obsessions? New rituals. New identities. New routines. New dopamine sources. Not just quitting something… but becoming someone new. ⸻ Jerry’s videos are ridiculous. But they also reveal something true: People are drawn to brands and creators who feel fully alive. And that usually requires a level of commitment most people are too afraid to embrace. ⸻ 💭 What brand or creator do you think commits to their identity better than anyone else online? ♻️ Repost this if it changed how you think about branding and content

Just as rotten wood crumbles under the carver’s tools instead of forming a beautiful sculpture, a person lacking integrity, discipline, or openness to growth may resist guidance, wisdom, or education. According to X’s own Help Centre, DMs support text, media, links, and even reactions – making them a genuinely useful channel for business communication.

🔹 AI should help people work smarter Walmart, we see AI as a way to remove manual, repetitive tasks so associates can focus on work that requires judgment, service and human connection.

🔹 Career pathways matter. As technology changes how work gets done, companies have an opportunity to choose to create pathways for associates to build new skills and move into growing roles.

What stays with me in moments like this isn’t the policy change. It’s the people behind it.
 
In too many rural communities, health care can feel stretched thin with limited resources, complex processes and real pressure on the people delivering care.
 
Care teams are often small, but deeply rooted in the places they serve. They’re not just providers — they’re neighbors, lifelines and a source of stability when everything else feels far away.
 
That’s why reducing administrative burden and speeding up payments matters. It’s giving time back to a nurse covering two roles. It’s helping a physician focus on a patient instead of paperwork. It’s helping rural hospitals stay strong for the communities that depend on them, while easing some of the financial pressure they face.
 
Because supporting the people who deliver care is how we make health care work better. Especially in the places that need it most.

Some of the most meaningful conversations I’ve had as a leader have been with mothers sharing what they needed, and too often didn’t receive, during pregnancy and childbirth.
 
For many families, this experience can feel overwhelming and difficult to navigate. For Black mothers, those challenges are too often compounded by real and persistent disparities. #BlackMaternalHealthWeek is a time to listen, reflect and act.
 
I've heard from women who wanted something simple but powerful: to feel supported, to be understood and to have someone by their side advocating for them.
 
Expanding access to doula support is one way we are working to make care more personal and more connected — helping mothers feel seen and supported before, during and after childbirth. This work is part of a bigger responsibility we have: to help make health care easier to navigate, more equitable and more affordable for the people we serve.
 
We know there is more work ahead. But listening, and turning what we hear into action, is how progress happens. Every mother deserves that support. Every family deserves a healthier start.

As Women’s History Month comes to a close, I’ve been taking a moment to reflect—not just on the month itself, but on the legacy we carry forward every day.
 
We stand on the shoulders of extraordinary women. Women like Marie Curie, who pushed the boundaries of science. Amelia Earhart, who redefined courage. Rosa Parks, who showed the quiet power of conviction. Katherine Johnson, whose brilliance helped launch humanity into space. Florence Nightingale, who transformed care through compassion and discipline. Mother Teresa, who embodied service. Jane Goodall, who taught us to listen more closely to the world around us.
 
And for me, this reflection is also deeply personal. I think about my mom—her resilience, her strength, and the example she set long before I understood what leadership really meant.
 
What connects all of these women isn’t just what they accomplished—it’s how they led. With purpose. With persistence. With a willingness to challenge what is and imagine what could be.
 
As leaders today, our responsibility is to carry that forward. To create space. To lift others. To lead in ways that make it easier for the next generation to rise even higher.
 
Women’s History Month may be ending, but the work—and the opportunity—continues.
 
Let’s keep going.

Raise your hand, opportunities are what you make them!

Today is National Intern Day. And right now, there are hundreds of incredibly bright and energetic young people wrapping up their summer at UnitedHealth Group. Drawn to our mission – to help people live healthier lives and help the health system work better for everyone – they’re gaining skills and experiences they’ll carry with them as they set out to do good in the world, here and beyond. 

My journey to health care started with an internship, too. I was fortunate to get a foot in the door of a Boston hospital. That summer, I was one of two interns working in the department. I was an undergrad. The other person was working on her master’s – and more than happy to brush all the grunt work my way. As it happens, she also helped me learn a most valuable lesson: Opportunities are what you make them.

One morning, our manager let us know there was a big meeting coming up. He asked if we could help. I raised my hand (she didn’t) and volunteered to stay late to put the briefing packets together, thinking maybe…just maybe...they’d let me come to the meeting. And they did. 

The next day, I showed up early in my red suit – my only suit – and found a seat. As the meeting got underway, one of our guests, the powerful Speaker of House for Massachusetts wrapped up his talk and asked if there were any questions. I took a deep breath, raised my hand and asked my question. Apparently, I made an impression. Because months later, he called the hospital. He was looking for someone to help him put together some focus groups and asked our boss, “what about that lady in the red suit?”
 
The rest of my career unfolded from there. 

If I hadn’t been willing to skip happy hour and stand at the copy machine working the three-hole punch, I might never have met a mentor who helped open a door to HR, which led to another door into law school, which led to a door to technology, and then another back to health care. 

So, as the summer intern season comes to a close, I want to extend my deepest appreciation to our incredible interns – for showing up with such great energy, perspective and a genuine eagerness to learn. It’s been truly inspiring to watch you grow. Keep showing up, keep raising your hands and keep building your networks, because you never know what opportunity will come your way. And remember this advice my mentor shared with me: “Be seen. Be heard. Be memorable.”

A few days after Valentine’s Day, I was reminded that “heart” isn’t just a symbol for love but for life. ❤️🧡

I was grateful to join the Heart-to-Heart event organized by our LEAD (Leading Employees of African Descent) employee resource group in observance of Black History Month and American Heart Month, raising awareness of chronic heart health within the Black community.

According to the American Heart Association, cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death for African Americans, with nearly 60% of Black adults (aged 20+) living with some form of CVD. During the session, our medical director Dr. Cara Pensabene, MD shared that prevention and management of cardiovascular disease start with awareness and access. Wellness benefits, like what we offer at Mastercard, support the mind, body, financial, and social well-being of our people. These are not “nice to have”; they reflect how we empower our employees to thrive, embracing flexibility and anchoring our culture in purpose and growth opportunities.

One key takeaway for me was this: even with full calendars, we have to be intentional about making time for self-care and focusing on what truly makes a difference. For me, that means moving more. I encourage you to prioritize your health and help spread awareness too.

#BlackHistoryMonth #AmericanHeartMonth #Wellbeing #WeAreMastercard

The Home Depot reports Q1 earnings on Tuesday. This is the housing economy's first big read of 2026. Wall Street expects same store sales down again. Most analysts are pricing in another tough quarter for the home improvement category. The story is bigger than that. If McDonald's K-shaped consumer thesis holds, Home Depot's quarter will tell us how it plays out in housing. The high income half of the K is renovating. Homeowners who locked in 3 percent mortgages aren't moving, but they're upgrading kitchens, replacing roofs, and building additions. Home Depot's Pro contractor business has been the strongest segment for two years because of exactly this dynamic. The lower income half of the K is deferring. Homeowners with adjustable rate loans, renters, and first time buyers priced out by 7 percent mortgages aren't doing discretionary home projects. Home Depot's DIY consumer segment captures this. Tuesday's split between Pro and DIY same store sales is the actual signal. If Pro grows and DIY shrinks, the K-shape is real in housing too. That tells every consumer business the bifurcation isn't just at the coffee counter or grocery shelf. It's structural. If Pro and DIY both decline, the high income consumer is finally pulling back. That changes the 2026 thesis for every brand selling discretionary goods to homeowners. Ted Decker has been Home Depot CEO since 2022. He doesn't speculate on the consumer. When he tells us what he's seeing in Pro versus DIY, listen. Tuesday at 6 a.m. Eastern. Watch the segment split first, total comp second.

In a recent conversation with one of our Business Resource Groups, I was asked about strategies for moving into #leadership roles and it made me reflect on the important distinction between being managed and being mentored.

Both are essential – managers help us succeed where we are, mentors help us prepare for what’s next.

Great managers build performance. They set clear goals, coach through challenges, hold people accountable and remove barriers to team success. 

Great mentors build perspective. They help you zoom out – think strategically about your growth, test ideas, and explore what’s next. A strong mentor challenges your assumptions and helps you see possibilities you might not see yourself. 

If you are aspiring to lead, or even just accelerate your own development, here’s where you can start:

– Find a mentor who checks the right boxes.
 □ Has the skills, judgment or influence you want to build
 □ Is known for developing others and consistently leading high-performing teams
 □ Will offer honest feedback, including the tough truths to push and support you
 □ Sits outside your reporting line to allow more freedom for curiosity and candid exploration

– Use the time with your mentor to discuss lessons learned from their experiences, both successes and setbacks, as well as what you’re currently experiencing. 

– Engage your manager in open conversation about your goals and how to create stretch opportunities.

– Pair your mentor’s perspective with your manager’s coaching for greatest impact.

And if you already lead, be both – a strong manager who develops people today, and a mentor who invests in the leaders of tomorrow. Results always matter, but the greatest legacy is leaving behind those truly ready to lead.

– Put the Wrench Down: Why ROI Starts with People – 
  
There’s a fine line between what we can do and what we should do. I learned that the hard way—not in the office, but under my kitchen sink on a Saturday morning.

With a wrench in hand and YouTube at my side, I was determined to fix a stubborn hot water valve. But I realized something: sure, I could try. But at what cost? A flooded kitchen? Hours wasted? Instead, I called a plumber.

That small moment reminded me of something far bigger—the curse of competence. Just because we’re capable doesn’t mean it’s the best use of our time, energy or expertise.

In #HR, this shows up everywhere. We tell ourselves, “It’s easier if I just do it myself.” 

But real impact comes when we invest in the right skills, empower others and align work where it belongs—whether that’s business partners driving outcomes, specialized experts elevating the function or colleague self-service.

Over my 30+ years in HR, I’ve seen our profession transform from administrators to business enablers. The greatest #ROI isn’t in doing everything ourselves—it’s in unlocking the potential of people and maximizing efficiency.

Sometimes the smartest move is to put the wrench down. Because when we stop trying to do it all, we create space for growth, innovation and real returns—on skills, on people and on business results.

September always feels like a reset – a reminder that none of us are ever too senior, too experienced or too established to keep learning. One of the most powerful, and sometimes overlooked, ways to grow is through #apprenticeship. 

At Thermo Fisher Scientific, we view apprenticeship as more than mentoring. It’s a two-way exchange between expert and learner, where both are developing, not just delivering. It’s a mutual investment built on trust, feedback and real-time collaboration.

—  For the expert, apprenticeship means sharing your thought process, creating scaffolds that empower independence, and coaching through real challenges – knowing when to step back so others can step up.
—  For the apprentice, it’s about watching closely, asking questions, articulating your reasoning and taking ownership of your growth. Over time, that practice builds both confidence and capability.

When done well, apprenticeship doesn’t just shape individuals – it builds a culture where learning is continuous, feedback is natural and teaching is everyone’s responsibility. That’s the kind of culture I want to be part of.

Looking back, I’ve been fortunate to experience both sides. I’ve learned the mechanics of a balance sheet from a former CFO and the basics of plumbing from my dad. Both shaped how I think, work and lead. And in turn, being able to teach others those same lessons has been one of the most rewarding experiences of my career – and my life.

As this new season begins, I invite you to reflect: What are you learning? Who are you teaching? And how can we each show up as both expert and apprentice?

Here’s to learning, always – together.

We all remember our first internship or job out of college.
