I had a lot to learn to effectively do that HR job, but a business leader saw potential in me and she helped me make the most of that experience. 

Over the course of my career in HR, I have found internships and other early talent roles to be very similar – a lot of raw talent and enthusiasm that just requires direction and thoughtful boundaries.   

So to all the recent grads starting their first career jobs this summer, or current students settling into their internships, I wanted to share some tips I wish I knew back then to make that development experience even stronger.  

 – Maximize your experience: Approach every task with enthusiasm and initiative. Your proactive attitude will not only enhance your experience but also demonstrate your potential to take on greater responsibilities. By treating every moment as a learning opportunity, the knowledge and skills you gain now will help build the foundation for your future success.

 – See the need, meet the need: With fresh eyes, you will see countless opportunities for improvement all around. Your perspectives can also help bring new solutions to a challenging problem. Think about the skills and experiences you bring and work with your manager to make a list of quick wins where you can have high impact. 

 – Be patient: Building skills and capabilities takes time – often longer than you think. When you consider the time it takes to understand the organization, build trust with stakeholders, and deliver on the responsibilities of your role, the growth happens on the journey – not in reaching the finish line. Focus on what experiences you need in the current role to prepare you for the next.

For some the trade off is worthy, for others (me included) not.

Today marks #WorldCancerDay, a day that hits close to home for me.

Cancer has affected my life in very personal ways—my dad fought prostate cancer for more than 17 years and my mom faced stage 3b breast cancer. And just last year, one of my routine screenings came back with an irregular result. Like so many people who face this type of unexpected news during their preventive screenings, my first reaction was fear. Thanks to Merck’s comprehensive benefits, I was able to quickly get follow-up testing and a biopsy — and fortunately, everything came back clear.

These tough moments remind me of how much access and support matter. That’s why I am so proud of the progress our company has made in support of cancer prevention and early detection. In under a year, we have expanded access to WHO-recommended screenings (breast, cervical, colorectal), HPV-related cancer vaccinations, and the time and flexibility to use these services—now reaching more than 96% of employees and their families across 71 countries. The team continues the hard work to extend these benefits where they are not yet available.  

I’m so grateful to everyone at Merck who made this possible and to all those working tirelessly to advance cancer prevention, early detection and care.

Q. What you have any inspirations for the look and style of the documentary?

When making the film I knew I wanted to draw on a lot of newspaper archived headlines and articles to showcase the changing attitudes towards the LGBT community, but I didn’t want it to be a flat and boring, glorified slide show with a voice over underneath. X/Twitter for SaaS Founders: The Distribution Playbook | Postory

May 26, 2026·11 min read

Key Takeaway

Learning how to grow on Twitter as a SaaS founder isn't about going viral. It's about picking three content pillars, writing in your real voice, replying where your buyers already are, and building a quiet funnel from X to email to trial to paid.

Most founders treat X like a billboard. They post a launch tweet, get a handful of likes from friends, and conclude the platform "doesn't work for B2B." The ones who win treat it as a distribution channel — a place where the few hundred people in your niche see your thinking, trust you over weeks, and sign up when they're ready. This post is the founder-specific playbook for exactly that: positioning, content pillars, the build-in-public tweet formula, reply targeting, and the funnel that turns attention into revenue.

## Why Is X Still the Best Distribution Channel for SaaS Founders?

X is still the best free distribution channel for SaaS founders because the people who buy software — developers, indie hackers, operators, and startup decision-makers — are concentrated there in a way no other platform matches. You don't need a million followers. You need the few hundred people in your niche to see your thinking repeatedly until they trust you. A single useful reply on a larger account's tweet can dramatically out-reach your own posts: founders routinely report a thoughtful reply pulling around 12,000 impressions versus 400 on an original post — roughly 30x the eyeballs. That asymmetry is the whole opportunity. Unlike paid ads, the cost is your time and your taste. Unlike SEO, it compounds in weeks, not quarters. And unlike LinkedIn, the tone rewards directness over polish — which suits a founder who'd rather build than market. The catch: it only works if you show up consistently and sound like a person, not a press release.

## What Are the 3 SaaS Content Pillars You Should Post About?

The three content pillars every SaaS founder should rotate through are Product, Story, and Insight — each doing a different job in the funnel. Product posts show the thing you're building in context (a feature solving a real problem, a before/after, a tiny demo clip). Story posts share the human journey: the bug that cost you a weekend, the churn that stung, the milestone that surprised you. Insight posts give away domain knowledge — opinions, frameworks, and lessons your buyers can use even if they never pay you. Most founders over-index on Product and wonder why nobody engages. The fix is a deliberate mix. A widely cited content ratio is roughly 80% value, 20% promotion— meaning Story and Insight should outnumber Product posts by a wide margin. The product still gets sold; it just rides in on content people actually want to read.

# Eliminate roles, not people: fine-tuning the talent search during times of change

Feature

Sep 13, 20237 mins

## Julia Anderson, chief technology and information officer at Campbell Soup Company, and Kristen Lamoreaux, president and CEO of recruitment firm Lamoreaux Search, join CIO.com’s Maryfran Johnson to discuss talent development, the benefits of shadow IT, and enabling a culture of support.

Having joined Campbell’s in January 2022, Julia Anderson’s enterprise-wide responsibilities run from digital workplace services, IT platforms, and architecture, to cybersecurity oversight, business analytics, and transformation projects and programs.

When she arrived, a business transformation was already underway. “There were two divisions structured and a central supply chain—very clear areas to partner with, but we weren’t set up to partner,” she says. “We were more of a services organization, so I had to create an organization that had architecture, data, and an analytics focus, but also digital partners. We make that our culture; to be together and succeed together with quick wins.”

When you come into an organization going through a transformation, skill sets can be deeply hidden, she adds. People have functional knowledge and technical capability, but because of different roles and operating models, they may have to be left out.

“We have to understand who our leaders and technical people are, and who can learn the new platforms and technologies being brought in and get things done,” she says. “Training becomes a big piece of it, too. I eliminate roles, not people. so what’s the prioritized work we need to do, and what capabilities do we need to do that work. Aside from that, other roles and other work have to stop. It can be uncomfortable when you explain it to people.”

With a different vantage point but similar sentiment, Kristen Lamoreaux leads a national IT recruitment firm that echoes her long-held personal and professional belief that every organization benefits from having more diverse and inclusive leadership teams.

And there are many different approaches to keep talent development thriving and functioning in a way to maintain a competitive edge. Providing access to data, reskilling, upskilling, and retaining all the best tech people—once you have them—is all part of the plan.

“One of the aspects of democratizing data and access, however, terrifies a lot of leaders because they think we can’t just give everybody access,” says Lamoreaux. “Of course you’re not, yet you create pathways and you can bring others in, because you never know where that next great idea is coming from. But make the space for the governance, and make sure people are understanding. You’re not going to let somebody jump into source code. It’s a matter of protecting what you can and giving access, creating those ramps.”

One of the biggest mistakes in HR transformation isn’t choosing the wrong AI model or platform.
 
It’s conceptual failure.
 
Many leaders in HR (and other disciplines, honestly) still think of AI as a distinct program or initiative. But AI isn't a program – it’s a permanent shift in how work gets done. That means cascading changes to everything from talent, to skills, to (entry-level) hiring.

P.S. You often hear that AI will automate rote tasks and unlock “higher-value work.” How do you define that higher-value work?

Thank you, Chip Cutter, for the conversation about HR and AI last week. (And congratulations to WSJ Leadership Institute on the inaugural CPO Council Summit!)
 
CPOs and CHROs are under intense pressure to undergo AI transformation. But what does success look like? We discussed how:
 
1. AI-powered productivity is the means, not the end. Growth is the end goal. Couple that extra time with talent for true results. This is why IBM is tripling entry-level hiring.
 
2. Value can be measured in (many) more ways than one, from time saved to downstream growth. On the flip side, remember: AI usage isn't free. Every query comes with a cost. 
 
3. No matter how sophisticated the technology becomes, HR leaders always need to prioritize the employee experience. Tech *in service of* the experience.
 
4. Please, please, please: Don't put agents on org charts. Especially if that technology isn't actually an agent.

What does AI mean for your talent strategy? How do you prepare for it?

Huge thanks to Paulo Carvao, former IBMer and Senior Fellow at Harvard University, for this great article in Forbes about how AI is redefining the future of work.

Here are my top three insights:

1️⃣ Economic growth through human-AI collaboration
AI delivers its greatest value when it augments, not replaces, human capabilities. Organizations that design work to combine human judgment with AI efficiency will see productivity gains that help fuel long-term growth.

2️⃣ Skills are the new competitive advantage
The rate and pace of technological change demand continuous learning. Both employees and employers alike must do their part to invest in the skills development necessary for future success.

3️⃣ Productivity with purpose
AI can automate tasks, but the real opportunity lies in freeing up employees to focus on the more strategic work that involves creativity, innovation and problem-solving, which drives differentiation and engagement.

How are you rethinking skills development and redesigning work in the AI Era? I’d love to hear your perspective. #AI #GenAI #skills

Growth isn’t always a straight line.

Years ago, I made a bold career move—I took a step back in my level and pay for a development opportunity. I left behind a role where I was the expert in HR to take a sales management role in which I knew very little. It was humbling. I had to rebuild credibility from scratch, and for a while, I struggled to even take myself seriously in this new role. Eventually, I anchored to what I do best: coaching for impact and making tough talent decisions that drive growth for individuals and the team. That’s when things started to shift. I learned that transferable skills and the ability to coach effectively matter more than a history of deep domain expertise.

I’m incredibly grateful to Adam Lenkowsky for seeing the potential in me, believing in my transferable skills, and reminding me that #UpIsNotTheOnlyWay.

This week, we hosted a global broadcast at Pfizer for Mental Health Awareness Month, and I was honored to be joined by the incredible Arianna Huffington for a conversation on all things mental health. We covered topics like the science of sleep, brain health, the power of physical connection, and how AI can help us reconnect with what makes us human.

Here are my top takeaways:

▪️ Stress is inevitable, but cumulative stress is avoidable. In as little as 60 seconds of conscious breathing, or focusing on something that brings you joy, you can interrupt the stress cycle. Small, consistent micro-steps will outlast big, unsustainable resolutions.
▪️ You can't pour from an empty cup. Whether you're a caregiver, a leader, or both, taking care of yourself isn't selfish — it's how you show up fully for the people who need you.
▪️ As AI becomes more capable, being human becomes more valuable. Resilience, empathy, creativity, and connection aren't soft skills anymore. They're the skills that matter most when intelligence alone is no longer a differentiator.

Thank you, Arianna, for a conversation that was both grounded in science and full of heart - you never fail to leave us with a renewed sense of optimism. And thank you to everyone who tuned in! 

#MentalHealthAwarenessMonth

Today – #internationalwomensday – is a day to reflect on all that women contribute to our communities and to our workplaces. 

While there’s still progress to make, women have come a long way in realizing greater equality and inclusion, both in society and at work. It’s important to take a moment to appreciate the progress made by those who came before us and commit ourselves to continuing this work. 

We can all make a difference. If you don’t feel included or have been treated unfairly, I encourage you have a direct conversation about what isn’t working and how it can get better.

I’ve been truly blessed to work with inspiring leaders over my career – women who helped shape the leader I am today. I appreciate their leadership and support. And I hope they are proud of me now, as I strive to pay it forward by doing for others, what they did for me.

A common thread connecting these leaders is a commitment to women helping women. I vividly remember the day a leader invited a few of us to her home to build a support network to help emerging leaders find balance as they grow their careers and their families at the same time. This kind of mentoring and support is critical to women advancing in the workplace.

I’m fortunate to work with an amazing leadership team at Wells Fargo. Many of them are women, and I hope they take a moment to reflect on where they are today, how they got here, and how they can help lift up the women in their lives.

Some of the most powerful innovations don’t start in a lab - they start in communities.

Years ago, Medtronic teams partnered locally in Ghana to help build a care platform designed around real community needs. It pairs community health workers with patients and uses an AI-enabled platform to monitor and guide care.

What started as a model used in Ghana is now supporting patients in Camden, New Jersey. Since 2023, 74 percent of patients with uncontrolled hypertension have seen improvement.

This is what happens when we listen first and design with humility - solutions scale while staying rooted in what matters most.

# Sammy Hemann’s Post

5d

Drink LMNT did over $200 million in revenue last year. They only raised about $6 million to do it. Most CPG brands burn that much in a single year of paid ads. LMNT built a nine-figure business on it and kept 20% net margins. The strategy was almost insultingly simple. Give the product away. LMNT started in 2019 when former research biochemist Robb Wolf kept hearing the same thing from his coaching clients: "I feel awful on a clean diet." The culprit wasn't the food, it was electrolytes. Whole-food and low-carb diets stripped out the processed foods most people got their sodium from. So Wolf built a sugar-free, high-sodium electrolyte mix to fix it. The product was good, but the growth engine was giving it away for free. LMNT's "Free 8-Pack" offer became the center of the entire business. You pay a few dollars in shipping, you get eight sample packets free. No catch. The logic underneath it is sharp. Electrolytes are a product you can't understand until you feel them. A description doesn't sell it, the experience does. So instead of spending money convincing strangers with ads, LMNT spent that money putting the actual product in their hands and letting their electrolytes close the sale. The math works because the lifetime value is enormous. Electrolytes are a daily habit. Once someone feels the difference and builds LMNT into their morning routine, they reorder for years. A few dollars of sample cost converts into a subscriber worth hundreds. The free pack isn't a discount, it's the most efficient ad they could possibly run. They stacked it with authority. LMNT became a fixture on Huberman Lab, The Drive, and Modern Wisdom, podcasts where the host actually uses the product and explains the science. No flashy campaigns. Just credible people explaining why electrolytes matter, then a free sample to prove it. The best marketing dollar is the one you spend letting people experience the product themselves. If your product is genuinely good, sampling isn't a cost. It's the highest-ROI channel you have. With chaange, I won’t be able to convince someone that a drink makes them think clearer. They have to feel it. The product has to do the convincing, which means the entire job is making something good enough that one can earns the second.

This is such an underrated growth strategy. So many brands obsess over CAC while LMNT basically turned product experience into the acquisition engine. The “give the product away” model works incredibly well when retention/LTV is strong enough to support it. Great work Sammy! Love following the growth!

The most productive thing you can do today? Embrace JOMO. We’ve all been raised on FOMO (Fear Of Missing Out), but in the corporate world, FOMO is just a polite term for a bottleneck.

If you feel the need to be in every 30-person meeting to "stay aligned," you aren't leading; you’re hovering. If you need to be CC'd on every email thread to "feel informed," you aren't empowering; you’re slowing the engine.

At Verizon, we are architecting an AI-enabled ecosystem to eliminate "the mundane". But tech alone won't give us speed. We need a cultural pivot from "Agreeable to Accountable".

JOMO - The Joy of Missing Out —is the ultimate leadership flex. * It’s the joy of trusting your team to take "Total Ownership" of the talent lifecycle without you in the room.

When we stop trying to be everywhere, we finally give our leaders the space to be innovative and quick. Speed doesn't come from more eyes on a project; it comes from fewer, more decisive ones.

Let’s stop rewarding "presence" and start rewarding "impact."
Who’s brave enough to decline that 4:00 PM "update" meeting and trust the team to handle it? That’s the BOLD standard.

If you lead a team, make check-ins part of your rhythm and rituals. Ask how people really are — and be ready to listen. Create the space, model the behaviors and show that care isn’t a policy — it’s an essential practice.

When we care for ourselves and each other, we build stronger teams, deepen trust and deliver better results. Because people who feel seen and supported bring their best — to work and to life.

Some of the best career advice I’ve ever received had nothing to do with strategy, skill-building or networking. It was this:

Be kind to yourself.

That sounds simple, but it’s harder than it looks—especially in a world that rewards speed, productivity and “always on” energy. We’re often quick to extend compassion to others but incredibly slow to give it to ourselves.

But the best leaders, teammates, and innovators I know all have one thing in common — they give themselves grace.

✨ Grace to learn without expecting perfection overnight.
✨ Grace to make mistakes without labeling everything as a failure.
✨ Grace to rest without feeling guilty.
✨ Grace to be human.

Here’s the truth—growth doesn’t happen in perfectly polished moments. It happens in the messy middle when projects don’t go to plan, when feedback stings, when we try something bold and it falls flat. That’s where the learning is. That’s where resilience gets built. 💪 

Listen, there are times when I get stuck on the lows and replay everything I should have done differently. But the emotional heaviness that comes with being your harshest critic is like mental quicksand — it traps your energy and rarely leads to anything productive.

Self-kindness isn’t about lowering the bar. It’s about creating the space we need to keep showing up—clear-minded, energized and ready to do our best work.

So here’s your gentle reminder:
✅ Celebrate the small wins—they add up.
✅ Don’t let one hard day erase months of progress.
✅ Speak to yourself the way you would to a friend who’s struggling.

Kindness fuels confidence. Grace fuels growth. And both are essential—not just for our careers, but for our well-being.

What’s one way you’ve given yourself grace recently?

One of the most important lessons I've learned in my career is the power of taking a real break.

It can be easy to celebrate constant hustle, always-on responsiveness, and squeezing just “one more thing” into the workday. But the truth is that results require rest. Creativity needs breathing room. Well-being demands boundaries.

At Verizon, we talk a lot about being our best for our customers, our colleagues and the communities we serve. That starts with being our best for ourselves. And that means knowing when to unplug. 

Whether it's stepping away for a vacation, signing off fully for the weekend, or just taking a walk between meetings—these moments of true rest are not “nice to have,” they’re essential. They give us the clarity and focus to lead well, solve problems creatively and support one another.

I recently took a few days off, and it was cleansing in so many ways. I could hear myself think and felt a sense of peace simply because I made the space to pause. 

Working endlessly is a direct path to burnout. Nothing will impact your efficiency and productivity more than draining every drop of your energy and attempting to push forward on fumes. My best ideas always come after I disconnect — not when I am running on empty. 

Here’s the catch. You need to make the time vs. take the time. It may sound like a subtle difference, but unless you carve out dedicated space to untether yourself from work, devices and whatever else you are juggling, it just won’t happen. Changing scenery is not enough. You need a full rest and reboot for it to count. 

Everyone needs to model this, especially if you’re a people leader. Your teams look up to you. If you don’t truly disconnect, they won’t either. So check in with your teams, talk openly about what you’re doing to step away and make sure they have a break within reach.  

I hope everyone reading this finds a chance this summer to really unplug, recharge and come back renewed. It’s one of the best investments we can make — in ourselves and in each other.

On Monday 27 April 2026, US service members at Naval Support Activity Bahrain began receiving WhatsApp messages on their personal phones. Signed Handala. The text:

"Your identities are fully known to our missile units. Soon you will be targeted by our Shahed drones and Kheibar missiles. We suggest you call your families now and say your final goodbyes."

The next day Handala — the cover identity for Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security, tracked as Storm-0842 — published the claimed personal details of 2,379 named US Marines. Rank. Unit. Home address. Family details. Daily commute. Shopping habits. Nightly leisure activities.

The security community's first instinct was to qualify the incident: the data was likely scraped from data brokers and social media rather than gathered from secure systems. That qualification reaches the opposite conclusion from the one intended.

If the targeting package for 2,379 named Marines was assembled from commercial sources rather than a breach, the threat is more serious, not less.

It means the intelligence collection system that produced personalised missile-threat messages required no exploit, no insider, no nation-state cyber capability, and no access to any classified system. It required a data broker account and a LinkedIn search.

This is the convergence article — the one that ties three previous DSI Chokepoint Doctrine pieces into a single argument:

→ The adtech surveillance piece: USCENTCOM confirmed targeting use of commercial location data, 14 April 2026.
→ The connected vehicle piece: the telemetry every modern car emits.
→ The Handala profile: who the actor is and what they do.

Three commercial data streams. One mosaic assembly. One personalised delivery channel — the most personal device in every Marine's pocket.

The adversary did not hack the military. It bought the data the military permitted its personnel to generate. That is the chokepoint no firewall closes.

If your organisation procures from any of the same data brokers — and most do — the same threat model applies to your executives, your board, and your operational personnel.

Whose name is in your supplier's catalogue this week?

Most people think a ₹600 restaurant meal is a better business than a ₹30 biscuit packet.

But structurally, businesses like Britannia and Nestlé often generate far higher returns with significantly lower capital intensity.

This is NOT truly an apple-to-apple comparison.

FMCG and restaurant businesses solve the same human need — food consumption — but through completely different economic models.

One scales through:
- distribution,
- repeat consumption,
- operating leverage,
- and brand habit.

The other scales through:
- physical expansion,
- service execution,
- customer experience,
- and location economics.

Britannia and Nestlé are already mature giants with limited growth runway.
Meanwhile, India’s QSR and restaurant industry may still be in the early innings of expansion.

The real question is:
Why do some business models structurally generate higher returns on capital than others?

Start creating for value.
Stay detatched from the outcome.

Divert all your energy into making something useful.

They always do.

Ces derniers jours sur LinkedIn, je vois de plus en plus de publications annonçant la “fin des ERP”.

Selon certains, avec l’IA, Claude Code, Lovable et les nouveaux outils de génération, il deviendrait bientôt inutile d’utiliser des ERP comme Divalto, Odoo, SAP ou Sage.

Honnêtement, je pense que la réalité est beaucoup plus nuancée.

Oui, l’IA va profondément transformer la manière de développer des logiciels.
Et c’est déjà en train de se produire.

Aujourd’hui, on peut :
➡️ développer beaucoup plus vite,
➡️ générer des interfaces en quelques minutes,
➡️ créer des workflows rapidement,
➡️ tester des idées plus facilement,
➡️ automatiser une partie du développement.

C’est une révolution technologique majeure.

Mais il y a une énorme différence entre :
👉 développer une petite application fonctionnelle,
et
👉 construire un ERP complet, robuste et capable de tenir pendant 10 ou 15 ans dans une entreprise.

Un ERP, ce n’est pas juste quelques écrans et une base de données.

C’est :

✔️ des dizaines d’années d’évolution,
✔️ des milliers de cas métiers gérés,
✔️ des contraintes réglementaires,
✔️ des problématiques de sécurité,
✔️ des enjeux de performance,
✔️ des mécanismes de traçabilité,
✔️ de la conformité légale,
✔️ des certifications,
✔️ des montées de version,
✔️ de la maintenance continue,
✔️ de l’interconnexion avec d’autres systèmes,
✔️ et surtout des milliers d’heures de retour terrain.

Développer seul une application avec l’IA n’a jamais été aussi accessible.
Et c’est une excellente chose.

Mais maintenir cette application dans le temps, la sécuriser, la faire évoluer, garantir sa stabilité, sa conformité et sa capacité à accompagner la croissance d’une entreprise… c’est une toute autre histoire.

Je pense que l’IA ne va pas remplacer les ERP.
En revanche, elle va profondément transformer la manière dont ils seront développés, personnalisés et intégrés.

Les éditeurs ERP qui sauront intégrer intelligemment l’IA dans leurs plateformes prendront probablement une énorme avance dans les prochaines années.

Et les intégrateurs ERP devront eux aussi évoluer :
✔️ moins de développement répétitif,
✔️ plus de conseil,
✔️ plus d’architecture,
✔️ plus d’accompagnement métier,
✔️ plus de vision globale des flux et des données.

L’IA va accélérer énormément de choses.
Mais construire un ERP fiable et durable restera encore longtemps un travail d’expérience, de méthode et de compréhension du terrain.

Et vous, pensez-vous que l’IA remplacera réellement les ERP historiques dans les prochaines années ? 👇

Ah, LinkedIn 🌈

All the scrolling of Instagram, but for people with lanyards.

Every second post seems to feature someone who is absolutely delighted to be attending a conference, thrilled to be moderating a panel, or honoured to be speaking at an event.

Maybe they are. Maybe I’ve been attending the wrong conferences all these years…  But if we’re honest, some of us are mostly delighted when the coffee is decent and we make it through the day without volunteering ourselves to sit on yet another steering group. 

This Pride Month, I’ve been thinking about authenticity.

Not corporate authenticity.
Not carefully curated content authenticity.
Not the kind that appears once a year when rainbow logos come out of storage.

You know… actual authenticity. 

The kind where people feel able to show up as themselves, admit when they don’t know something, and occasionally acknowledge that they are not, in fact, delighted by every aspect of professional life.

I’m generally not known for sitting quietly on the fence.

Sometimes that’s served me well.
Sometimes it’s got me into trouble.

But I’ve always believed leadership starts with being genuine. People don’t need polished perfection. They need honesty, integrity, and a reasonable chance that the person they’re talking to is the same person they’d meet over a coffee.

Rainbow logos have their place.

Visibility matters.
Representation matters.
Seeing organisations publicly support LGBT+ people matters.

But perhaps the challenge for all of us is moving from ‘rainbow washing’ visibility for profit to visibility for purpose.

Not asking, “How will this make us look?”

But asking, “How will this help people feel seen, valued and included?”

Belonging is what happens after the social media posts are written. It’s created through everyday conversations, leadership decisions, workplace cultures and communities where people feel able to show up as themselves without feeling the need to edit themselves to belong.

Not just during Pride Month.

En byrå i Köpenhamn mejlade mig igår.

“Vi hittade dig på LinkedIn.”
Det är en mening som inte hade existerat för två år sedan.

För två år sedan var jag i princip osynlig här. Jag publicerade sällan något, hade ingen tydlig strategi och såg LinkedIn mest som ett digitalt CV.

Sedan började jag dela med mig av det jag faktiskt kan.
Inte sälja. Dela.
Tankar om voice over. Erfarenheter från studion. Små insikter om hur en röst påverkar ett budskap.
Inget av det blev viralt.

Men jag fortsatte ändå.
Igår fick jag alltså ett mejl från en byrå i Köpenhamn. De berättade att de hade sett mina inlägg här på LinkedIn. När de behövde en svensk röst till en nordisk kampanj fanns jag redan på deras radar.

Inte för att jag hade skickat ett säljmejl.
Inte för att jag hade köpt annonser.
Utan för att jag hade dykt upp regelbundet med något som var relevant för dem.

Det är lätt att tro att synlighet handlar om räckvidd.
Jag tror att det handlar mer om igenkänning.

Och igenkänning bygger förtroende.
Så om du funderar på att börja dela med dig av det du kan - börja.

Du vet aldrig vem som läser idag och hör av sig om sex månader.

🚀 Day 83/100 – LeetCode Daily Challenge

📌 Problem: 3753. Total Waviness of Numbers in Range II
🔗 https://lnkd.in/gSdC8Ugb

💡 Approach:
- The range can be extremely large, making brute-force enumeration impossible.
- Used Digit DP to count numbers and their total waviness efficiently.
- Process digits from left to right while maintaining:
 • Current position
 • Previous digits
 • Tight constraint (whether the prefix matches the limit)
 • Accumulated waviness count
- For each middle digit, determine whether it forms:
 • A peak (greater than both neighbors), or
 • A valley (smaller than both neighbors).
- Memoize DP states to avoid recomputation.
- Compute total waviness from 0 to num2 and subtract the result from 0 to num1−1.

✅ Time Complexity: O(D × States × 10)

✅ Space Complexity: O(States)

Your LinkedIn profile is either a door or a wall. Most are walls.

Here's how you know which one yours is:

A wall profile:
Generic headline that reads like a job title, about section that lists skills instead of telling a story
No recent posts or activity
No clear indication of who you help or how
Makes the visitor work to understand what you do

A door profile:
Headline that says exactly who you help and how
About section that speaks directly to your ideal client or employer
Regular posts that demonstrate your thinking
Clear services or portfolio
Makes the visitor feel like they've already started a conversation

The difference is not talent. It's not experience. It's intentionality.
Most people set up their LinkedIn once and leave it. A door profile is something you build deliberately with your specific audience in mind, updated as you grow.

If someone landed on your profile right now and spent 30 seconds on it, what would they conclude?

That's your answer.

Yesterday, I crossed 10,000 followers on LinkedIn! 🥳

And somewhere along the way, this community became my favourite part of the internet.

10,000 people here now.

Honestly, that means a lot.

Because when I started posting on LinkedIn, I wasn’t trying to become a creator or build an audience.

I just wanted to make ESG and sustainability less overwhelming for businesses that genuinely want to do better, but don’t know where to begin.

And somewhere along the way, 10,000 people stayed for those conversations.

Founders.
ESG professionals.
Teams navigating GHG Accounting and BRSR for the first time.
People trying to understand how sustainability actually works beyond reports and buzzwords.

A few years ago, I probably looked at companies very differently.

During my Master’s in Environmental Economics, we were taught to see companies through a very critical lens, that growth and capitalism often come at the cost of people and the environment.

Then I started working with companies directly.

And my perspective changed.

Most companies are not intentionally trying to do harm.
Many are simply trying to balance business realities while figuring out what responsible growth should actually look like.

That belief became one of the foundations of PlanetaryPlus.

Not as a company that “calls out” businesses, but as someone who can work with them, guide them, and help them move from confusion to clarity. 

And honestly, that’s why this community means so much to me.

Because the conversations here have always been thoughtful, practical, and hopeful.

Especially now, when more Indian businesses are no longer asking:
“Do we need to care about ESG?”

They’re asking:
“How do we do this properly?”

That shift is important.

We still have a long way to go, but I genuinely believe more companies today want to build responsibly than we give them credit for.

Thank you to everyone who reads, shares, discusses, questions, or contributes here in any way.

10,000 is just a number.

But the people behind it make this space meaningful.

За 4 года я разобрал больше профилей, чем помню. На эфирах, в личных консультациях, с клиентами. И паттерн как правило всегда один: не одна ошибка, а 5:

🔹 Headline продаёт не ту роль или вообще не продаёт
🔹 Локация и Open to Work настроены против тебя, а не за
🔹 About написан “чтоб покороче”, а нужно наоборот
🔹 Рекомендаций нет или одна, а это бесплатное доверие
🔹 Стратегия размыта: “PM или продакт или аналитик - куда возьмут”. То есть никуда

Я устал повторять эти 5 вещей по сто раз. Поэтому собрал AI-агента, который говорит их за меня. Моим тоном, с конкретикой вместо «улучшите Headline». Агент обучен на дестяких моих видео и нескольких сотен тысяч строк текста.

Как это будет работать7?

Загружаешь PDF своего LinkedIn, агент смотрит на профиль глазами рекрутера + учитывает все последние тренды и алгоритмы Linkedin и выдаёт разбор: вердикт, что уже хорошо, а что нужно улучшить (5-8 конкретных правок, топ-3 приоритета) плюс скрытый потенциал.

Не “вам стоит лучше описать раздел About”, а «убери Project Manager, поставь Engineering Manager через слэш, смени локацию на Лондон, добавь нужные локации в Open to Work». То, что я сказал бы лично во время прожарки.

Открываю закрытую бету на 10 человек. Бесплатно. От вас взамен честная обратная связь: что попало, что нет, где тон промахнулся. 

Мне это нужно, чтобы решить, делать агента публичным или оставить в личном сопровождении.

Что нужно сделать. Просто напишите любой комментарий к посту и в течение дня выберу 10 человек, напишу в личку и мы вместе пройдемся по алгоритму

# AstraZeneca's Baxfendy Approved for Hypertension Treatment

Medical Devices--Pharmaceutical--Biotechnology

2w

A genuinely meaningful approval for one of the most undertreated conditions in medicine. The FDA has approved AstraZeneca's Baxfendy, a first-of-its-kind once-daily tablet for adults whose hypertension remains inadequately controlled despite taking multiple medications. 1.4 billion people worldwide have hypertension, and tens of millions of U.S. patients still struggle with elevated blood pressure even on two or more antihypertensive drugs. What makes Baxfendy different is its mechanism. Rather than working like any existing therapy, it inhibits an enzyme that synthesizes aldosterone, a hormone that raises blood pressure by signaling the body to retain water and salt while excreting potassium. The late-stage trial enrolled patients with persistently hard-to-control blood pressure and showed two doses were each significantly better than placebo, with a generally clean tolerability profile. AstraZeneca CEO Pascal Soriot has called it a big product, with executives projecting at least $5 billion in peak annual sales, potentially growing to $10 billion if the drug succeeds in additional studies including chronic kidney disease. The drug is expected in pharmacies by June 9. Mineralys Therapeutics, which is advancing its own drug with the same mechanism, saw shares dip 3% on the news, though analyst Dennis Ding at Jefferies noted the approval may actually be constructive for Mineralys in terms of partnering discussions by establishing labeling and payer access visibility for the drug class. A new chapter in blood pressure management is officially open.#Pharma#Hypertension#CardiovascularHealth#FDAApproval#AstraZeneca

Most people think a ₹600 restaurant meal is a better business than a ₹30 biscuit packet.

But structurally, businesses like Britannia and Nestlé often generate far higher returns with significantly lower capital intensity.

This is NOT truly an apple-to-apple comparison.

FMCG and restaurant businesses solve the same human need — food consumption — but through completely different economic models.

One scales through:
- distribution,
- repeat consumption,
- operating leverage,
- and brand habit.

The other scales through:
- physical expansion,
- service execution,
- customer experience,
- and location economics.

Britannia and Nestlé are already mature giants with limited growth runway.
Meanwhile, India’s QSR and restaurant industry may still be in the early innings of expansion.

The real question is:
Why do some business models structurally generate higher returns on capital than others?

Ces derniers jours sur LinkedIn, je vois de plus en plus de publications annonçant la “fin des ERP”.

Selon certains, avec l’IA, Claude Code, Lovable et les nouveaux outils de génération, il deviendrait bientôt inutile d’utiliser des ERP comme Divalto, Odoo, SAP ou Sage.

Honnêtement, je pense que la réalité est beaucoup plus nuancée.

Oui, l’IA va profondément transformer la manière de développer des logiciels.
Et c’est déjà en train de se produire.

Aujourd’hui, on peut :
➡️ développer beaucoup plus vite,
➡️ générer des interfaces en quelques minutes,
➡️ créer des workflows rapidement,
➡️ tester des idées plus facilement,
➡️ automatiser une partie du développement.

C’est une révolution technologique majeure.

Mais il y a une énorme différence entre :
👉 développer une petite application fonctionnelle,
et
👉 construire un ERP complet, robuste et capable de tenir pendant 10 ou 15 ans dans une entreprise.

Un ERP, ce n’est pas juste quelques écrans et une base de données.

C’est :

✔️ des dizaines d’années d’évolution,
✔️ des milliers de cas métiers gérés,
✔️ des contraintes réglementaires,
✔️ des problématiques de sécurité,
✔️ des enjeux de performance,
✔️ des mécanismes de traçabilité,
✔️ de la conformité légale,
✔️ des certifications,
✔️ des montées de version,
✔️ de la maintenance continue,
✔️ de l’interconnexion avec d’autres systèmes,
✔️ et surtout des milliers d’heures de retour terrain.

Développer seul une application avec l’IA n’a jamais été aussi accessible.
Et c’est une excellente chose.

Mais maintenir cette application dans le temps, la sécuriser, la faire évoluer, garantir sa stabilité, sa conformité et sa capacité à accompagner la croissance d’une entreprise… c’est une toute autre histoire.

Je pense que l’IA ne va pas remplacer les ERP.
En revanche, elle va profondément transformer la manière dont ils seront développés, personnalisés et intégrés.

Les éditeurs ERP qui sauront intégrer intelligemment l’IA dans leurs plateformes prendront probablement une énorme avance dans les prochaines années.

Et les intégrateurs ERP devront eux aussi évoluer :
✔️ moins de développement répétitif,
✔️ plus de conseil,
✔️ plus d’architecture,
✔️ plus d’accompagnement métier,
✔️ plus de vision globale des flux et des données.

L’IA va accélérer énormément de choses.
Mais construire un ERP fiable et durable restera encore longtemps un travail d’expérience, de méthode et de compréhension du terrain.

Et vous, pensez-vous que l’IA remplacera réellement les ERP historiques dans les prochaines années ? 👇

Ah, LinkedIn 🌈

All the scrolling of Instagram, but for people with lanyards.

Every second post seems to feature someone who is absolutely delighted to be attending a conference, thrilled to be moderating a panel, or honoured to be speaking at an event.

Maybe they are. Maybe I’ve been attending the wrong conferences all these years…  But if we’re honest, some of us are mostly delighted when the coffee is decent and we make it through the day without volunteering ourselves to sit on yet another steering group. 

This Pride Month, I’ve been thinking about authenticity.

Not corporate authenticity.
Not carefully curated content authenticity.
Not the kind that appears once a year when rainbow logos come out of storage.

You know… actual authenticity. 

The kind where people feel able to show up as themselves, admit when they don’t know something, and occasionally acknowledge that they are not, in fact, delighted by every aspect of professional life.

I’m generally not known for sitting quietly on the fence.

Sometimes that’s served me well.
Sometimes it’s got me into trouble.

But I’ve always believed leadership starts with being genuine. People don’t need polished perfection. They need honesty, integrity, and a reasonable chance that the person they’re talking to is the same person they’d meet over a coffee.

Rainbow logos have their place.

Visibility matters.
Representation matters.
Seeing organisations publicly support LGBT+ people matters.

But perhaps the challenge for all of us is moving from ‘rainbow washing’ visibility for profit to visibility for purpose.

Not asking, “How will this make us look?”

But asking, “How will this help people feel seen, valued and included?”

Belonging is what happens after the social media posts are written. It’s created through everyday conversations, leadership decisions, workplace cultures and communities where people feel able to show up as themselves without feeling the need to edit themselves to belong.

Not just during Pride Month. 
All year round, thanks. 🌈

🚀 Day 83/100 – LeetCode Daily Challenge

📌 Problem: 3753. Total Waviness of Numbers in Range II
🔗 https://lnkd.in/gSdC8Ugb

💡 Approach:
- The range can be extremely large, making brute-force enumeration impossible.
- Used Digit DP to count numbers and their total waviness efficiently.
- Process digits from left to right while maintaining:
 • Current position
 • Previous digits
 • Tight constraint (whether the prefix matches the limit)
 • Accumulated waviness count
- For each middle digit, determine whether it forms:
 • A peak (greater than both neighbors), or
 • A valley (smaller than both neighbors).
- Memoize DP states to avoid recomputation.
- Compute total waviness from 0 to num2 and subtract the result from 0 to num1−1.

✅ Time Complexity: O(D × States × 10)

✅ Space Complexity: O(States)

Yesterday, I crossed 10,000 followers on LinkedIn! 🥳

And somewhere along the way, this community became my favourite part of the internet.

10,000 people here now.

Honestly, that means a lot.

Because when I started posting on LinkedIn, I wasn’t trying to become a creator or build an audience.

I just wanted to make ESG and sustainability less overwhelming for businesses that genuinely want to do better, but don’t know where to begin.

And somewhere along the way, 10,000 people stayed for those conversations.

Founders.
ESG professionals.
Teams navigating GHG Accounting and BRSR for the first time.
People trying to understand how sustainability actually works beyond reports and buzzwords.

A few years ago, I probably looked at companies very differently.

During my Master’s in Environmental Economics, we were taught to see companies through a very critical lens, that growth and capitalism often come at the cost of people and the environment.

Then I started working with companies directly.

And my perspective changed.

Most companies are not intentionally trying to do harm.
Many are simply trying to balance business realities while figuring out what responsible growth should actually look like.

That belief became one of the foundations of PlanetaryPlus.

Not as a company that “calls out” businesses, but as someone who can work with them, guide them, and help them move from confusion to clarity. 

And honestly, that’s why this community means so much to me.

Because the conversations here have always been thoughtful, practical, and hopeful.

Especially now, when more Indian businesses are no longer asking:
“Do we need to care about ESG?”

They’re asking:
“How do we do this properly?”

That shift is important.

We still have a long way to go, but I genuinely believe more companies today want to build responsibly than we give them credit for.

Thank you to everyone who reads, shares, discusses, questions, or contributes here in any way.

10,000 is just a number.

But the people behind it make this space meaningful.

Were I ever to need an authorly Facebook profile, I think I would create a new one and hide the current one, because I like having that only for family, friends, and basically only people I've met face-to-face.

Rachel Olsen: Why I Use Twitter

Are you on Twitter? I'm not sure how long I've been on Twitter, but I do know it didn't take long for Twitter to become my favorite form of social media. When I first joined the ranks of those who speak in 140 characters or less, lots of people asked me the same question: Why? In fact, they often phrased it in the same way, "Why do you care to hear what people had for lunch?"

They were making a huge assumption that all anyone ever did on Twitter was say, "I just had a chicken-salad sandwich." Or, "Running carpool to the baseball field now." I'd answer their question by explaining, "The people I follow don't tell me what they had for lunch." The people I choose to follow on Twitter give me helpful information.

- They tell me which products or technologies have worked best for them.
- They tell me what they've read recently that's worth seeing, and give the link.
- They tell me what's going on in their industries. And in my industry.
- They tweet Bible verses or share their insight into the gospel.
- They answer my questions when I ask.
- They keep me abreast on breaking news.
- They tweet inspiring quotes.
- They make me laugh.
- They alert me when there's a new post on their blog - giving the topic and link should I be interested.

All this in a short, digestible, easy to skim format. I use TweetDeck to organize the tweets of those I follow. I sort people into lists with a separate column for each list: Publishing industry folks, P31 girlfriends, Insightful pastors, etc. Twitter and TweekDeck have pretty much replaced blog subscriptions, Google Reader, and RSS feeds for me. And I waste less time Internet browsing now that I'm on Twitter. Still don't believe Twitter is helpful? Check this:

By the way, I really want to know what book that guy is reading - it must be compelling! So that's why I use Twitter. Because it's helpful, useful, entertaining and very doable for me. I do have to confess that a couple months ago I started following some fellow foodies on Twitter. These are serious food industry types. And they sometimes do tweet what they had for lunch. Believe me their lunches are interesting! So now I have to revise my answer to the "Why do you care what people had for lunch" question. My new answer is, "That's the beauty of Twitter. It gives you instant access to the people and information that YOU would like to have access to." Twitter is like the world's coffee shop. Day or night there's community and conversation going on. And all you need is a twitter handle - and maybe a hashtag - to find the people you'd like to chat with and jump into the conversation. Stay awhile and sip a latte, or just get your coffee to go. So are you on Twitter? If so, who are some of your favorite people to follow? You can follow me at@RachelOlsen.

NU Social IMC: Alison Solway

All marketing mangers working in a retail environment know the importance of their customers; after all without them there is no business. But now, through the advent of social media, it’s possible to leverage these customers even more, and get them to want to work for you—for free.

Social communities are popping up all over the web, and it’s easy for department stores to see why and be encouraged to get onboard. Social communities draw valuable insights and information from customers. In the competitive department store environment, forming a social community is the best way to distinguish your store for the competition. While communities aren’t always appropriate for certain types of businesses, they are a wonderful resource for any business that ignites passion. And as the old saying goes, fashion is passion.

A fashion community can take on a variety of different forms, from news and resources, to a Pinterest type community where members can share fashion ideas and make look-books. It’s up to the retailer to figure out what is the best format, but the possibilities are endless and exciting.

So how do you get started?

1. Before launching the community its important to monitor your target market and listen to what they’re already talking about online. This can help you create buzz worthy topics by building off of their interests. Radian6 and Netbase are both wonderful tools for social media monitoring.

2. Have a big event to let people know that the community exists. Suggestions include a webinar, an online deal or discount for those who join, or an online chat with a famous designer. And don’t forget to promote it in your stores!

3. It is important that the community host allows the conversation to flow freely. Initially, your store will have to have to facilitate the discussion but then it’s important to allow the community members take over. This community will obviously be fashion related, so listen carefully to what they’re saying. These insights can help determine what customers want to see in your store, what they will be buying, and how much of it.

4. Keep it sustainable. The community has to be long lasting, so it’s important to set up the community to be an ongoing resource for your customers. Shopping itself is a continuous social activity between women, so the community can easily be too. It is important to remember to keep the information timely and relevant to your brand.

In addition to seeing an increase in sales, you can check the ROI of your community. All you have to do is password protect the community site, and compare the names against your current database. If customers are purchasing from your website for the first time but are community members, its likely that the community is driving the sale.

## Why

Agents need an easy way to pull their own-account data from Twitter — own posts, own likes, own profile — without having to know or hardcode their own handle. WAWQAQ flagged today that `opencli twitter tweets` currently rejects no-username calls (must pass screen name explicitly), and asked for a consistency pass over all twitter read commands.

## Primary change — `clis/twitter/tweets.js`

- `username` arg switched from `required: true` to optional.
- When no username is given, detect the logged-in user via the AppTabBar profile link on `https://x.com/home` (same pattern already used in `twitter/profile` and `twitter/likes`).

## Consistency pass — `profile.js` / `likes.js` / `following.js` / `followers.js`

The default-self pattern in these four siblings was already in code but silently broken: `page.evaluate()` primitive returns come back through the CDP bridge wrapped as `{session: 'site:twitter', data: '/ '}` (same envelope root cause as #1525). The adapters were calling `.replace()` directly on the envelope object → `TypeError` → bubbled up as `AUTH_REQUIRED 'Could not detect logged-in user'`, even for users that were correctly logged in.

Fix per file:

1. **Wrap the AppTabBar probe with `unwrapBrowserResult`** so the bare href string survives the CDP envelope.
2. **Add explicit `page.goto('/home') + page.wait(primaryColumn)`** before the probe in `likes` / `following` — the framework pre-nav lands on bare `x.com` and the AppTabBar sidebar is not always mounted there.
3. **`following.js`: switch probe from function-literal `() => {...}` to template-string form.** Live-confirmed via debug probe: the function-literal form silently drops primitive return values entirely — the bridge returns `{session: 'site:twitter'}` with no `data` field at all, while the template-string form returns `{session, data: '/jakevin7'}` as expected. Same daemon-side bug class as #1525.

By comparing the tracking on his retweet URLs to tracking on the original URL, he discovered that links in retweets often garnered more traffic than the original tweets. From a business perspective, this points to the idea that, with Twitter, your customers can be your best advertisers. People are more likely to look at something if someone who isn't trying to make money off of you sends you a link. Self-promotion can get you only so far.

If you have a business Twitterfeed, why not stream it to your home page? It's a simple widget that you can add with minimal customization, and it will further humanize your brand/business, create a more dynamic site, and make your customers part of what's going on.

## Easy way to get involved in conversations

Just search for a question mark! You'll end up with a whole bunch of tweeted questions. Just reply and join the conversation!

On bounced rent cheques and teary-eyed excuses: Solway wins A.M. Klein Prize

Congratulations to David Solway, who has won the A.M. Klein Prize for Poetry for Reaching for Clear: The Poetry of Rhys Savarin. This is a strong collection of poems, as much for what it does not have as for what it does. It's rich in imagery, craft and language and free of the obtuse diction and references that has made some of his past poetry somewhat opaque. Solway's last three books of poetry have been in assumed (approriated) voices, in which he takes on a personnage and imagines a complete biographical, historical, geographical, cultural and linguistic setting. You have to be uniquely skilled to accomplish this as convincingly as Solway does. We seem to be seeing more and more works that use this approach, for example Stephen Marche's latest book, a fictional literary anthology titled Shining at the Bottom of the Sea. I wonder if this is an emerging trend as immigrant writers increasingly gain mainstream prominence and win prizes(particularly writers from warm climes, the Carribean, South Asia.) Post-immigrant writers seem to be searching for an authenticity in more traditional, pre-colonial cultures, or at least they seem to be seeking out a socio-cultural tension that no longer exists for them and their generation. It's a reversal of the typical immigrant desire to conform and gain acceptance in their chosen, adopted home. Now local writers want to seek faraway, foreign cultural terrain to reinvigorate their imaginations.

Tough times have a way of sharpening your perspective and reshaping how you think about resilience.

This was me, living with breast cancer in 2020. Having since recovered, I realised it was never about speed - and neither was reaching Everest Base Camp. Both were journeys where mindset mattered and where the harder moments called for focus and resolve.

Treatment taught me to slow down, respect my limits, and keep moving when progress felt uncertain. Training for the trek felt much the same. Some days were strong. Others were simply about showing up and putting one foot in front of the other.

What stayed with me was how similar recovery and the climb really are. Resilience isn’t about pushing nonstop. It’s about good judgement, staying clear on what matters, and keeping things moving when the road gets harder.

I’m deeply grateful to my family, especially my son, Finlay, who joined the trek, and to the friends and volunteers who supported me along the way. None of this is ever done alone.

For me, resilience shows up in how I lead day to day. Staying grounded. Making thoughtful choices. And sometimes, when the moment comes, resilience is about finishing strong.

One of the things I love about Twitter is that it is up to us to decide how we want to use it. I want to share with you a variety of different tips. All of these are based on how I use Twitter. Hopefully you'll discover at least one new thing & find it worth sharing with your own followers.

Replies on Twitter

About 10 days ago Twitter made a change in how replies are handled. Replies are tweets that start with @username. Previously you had the options (via your settings) whether or not you wanted to see replies your followers make to those you are not following or not. Now you can only see replies your followers make to those you are also following.

Twitter claims that only 3% of users had this feature enabled. Personally, I think that those 3% were likely amongst the most active users. In any event, being able to see @replies was great for those of us who are looking to expand our network, find more like-minded people and to be able to find others to engage with. As my own follower base grew, I know that it helped a lot of my own followers connect with others. Now when I have an exchange with someone that I think may interest other followers, I will RT their tweet and respond to that or I will reply and put a "." in front of their user name.

The change in replies has made #followfriday a bit of a mess. Even though we've now had our second Friday since the change, many of the more active users don't understand how making recommendations to others is almost pointless if they start with @username. The reason is that only that person, those following that person already and anyone else mentioned in the tweet will see the recommendation. A way around it is to start off with anything other than @username.

Retweet is King

Aside from exchanges on Twitter, one of the great things about it is the ability to share information. Retweeting is used to pass along useful things you see your own followers tweet.

If you are a follower of mine, you'll see that I do a considerable number of retweets each day. I do it not just to pass along information to others but also so that my own followers can find other people that share useful information on Twitter.

I don't suggest going retweet crazy but try and take the time to share information you think others may be interested in. The benefit of retweeting others is that your own followers will see you do it and you just may find your own tweets get retweeted more often.

There are 2 ways to handle retweets:

RT @username [Tweet]

[Tweet] via @username

In both cases, make sure to include a space before the @username so that the person you are retweeting will see it (and it will also make their profile clickable for your followers).

I personally prefer using the second method. This makes it easier for tweets I pass along to catch the eye of those following me.

Always Acknowledge

X/Twitter for SaaS Founders: The Distribution Playbook | Postory

May 26, 2026·11 min read

Key Takeaway

Learning how to grow on Twitter as a SaaS founder isn't about going viral. It's about picking three content pillars, writing in your real voice, replying where your buyers already are, and building a quiet funnel from X to email to trial to paid.

Most founders treat X like a billboard. They post a launch tweet, get a handful of likes from friends, and conclude the platform "doesn't work for B2B." The ones who win treat it as a distribution channel — a place where the few hundred people in your niche see your thinking, trust you over weeks, and sign up when they're ready. This post is the founder-specific playbook for exactly that: positioning, content pillars, the build-in-public tweet formula, reply targeting, and the funnel that turns attention into revenue.

## Why Is X Still the Best Distribution Channel for SaaS Founders?

X is still the best free distribution channel for SaaS founders because the people who buy software — developers, indie hackers, operators, and startup decision-makers — are concentrated there in a way no other platform matches. You don't need a million followers. You need the few hundred people in your niche to see your thinking repeatedly until they trust you. A single useful reply on a larger account's tweet can dramatically out-reach your own posts: founders routinely report a thoughtful reply pulling around 12,000 impressions versus 400 on an original post — roughly 30x the eyeballs. That asymmetry is the whole opportunity. Unlike paid ads, the cost is your time and your taste. Unlike SEO, it compounds in weeks, not quarters. And unlike LinkedIn, the tone rewards directness over polish — which suits a founder who'd rather build than market. The catch: it only works if you show up consistently and sound like a person, not a press release.

## What Are the 3 SaaS Content Pillars You Should Post About?

The three content pillars every SaaS founder should rotate through are Product, Story, and Insight — each doing a different job in the funnel. Product posts show the thing you're building in context (a feature solving a real problem, a before/after, a tiny demo clip). Story posts share the human journey: the bug that cost you a weekend, the churn that stung, the milestone that surprised you. Insight posts give away domain knowledge — opinions, frameworks, and lessons your buyers can use even if they never pay you. Most founders over-index on Product and wonder why nobody engages. The fix is a deliberate mix. A widely cited content ratio is roughly 80% value, 20% promotion— meaning Story and Insight should outnumber Product posts by a wide margin. The product still gets sold; it just rides in on content people actually want to read.

Curiosity doesn’t fade with experience. If anything, it becomes more important over time. I had a really thoughtful conversation this week about careers, curiosity and what actually keeps people motivated – and it left me reflecting on a few things.

Curiosity still matters: probably more than ever. 

Not curiosity for curiosity’s sake, but that instinct to ask questions, look beyond your own role, and really understand people, context and what’s changing around you. Especially now, when AI can take on so much of the “task” work.

Purpose is what gets people out of bed – and keeps them coming back.

People don’t come to work just for tasks or titles. They come for learning, connection and to feel part of something that matters. If organisations want the next generation to show up, stay curious and keep growing, we have to create cultures that don’t knock that instinct out of them.

Careers aren’t neat.

They’re built on a mix of hard work, capability and opportunity – and having the confidence to say yes, or ask the question. If you don’t ask, you don’t get. That hasn’t changed – and I don’t think it ever will.

And while AI will change how we work, it won’t replace what matters most.

The first mile – starting a conversation, spotting an idea, being brave enough to reach out. And the final mile – building trust, relationships and follow‑through. That’s still human territory.

One final reflection: leadership only works if you stay close to the real work.

If you’re not spending time with the people doing the job, listening to what’s working and what isn’t, it’s very easy to slip into assumption rather than reality.

Today, as we celebrate the progress women have made around the world for #IWD, I can’t help but think about the girls and women who are living through conflict, not on the margins of the story, but right at the centre of it. Across conflicts around the world, women are among those most affected by wars they did not choose.

A few grounding facts, hard to read, but important to face, drawn from the work of the UN and its humanitarian agencies:

• In Afghanistan, women are now excluded from almost every part of public life. Following new restrictions in late 2024, no girls are expected to be in secondary education, according to UN reporting, making Afghanistan the only country where this is the case.

• In Gaza, UN Women reports that more than a million women are facing catastrophic hunger, reflecting the devastating humanitarian impact these sorts of conflicts have on civilians.

• Across parts of West and Central Africa affected by violence and climate shocks, women and children make up around 80% of refugees and asylum seekers, according to UNHCR.

• In Ukraine, UN agencies report that nearly 6.7 million women need humanitarian assistance, gender‑based violence has increased significantly, and years of progress on equality have been rolled back by the war.

Behind every statistic is a human story, lives shaped by disrupted childhoods, lost education, forced displacement and the quiet, relentless work of holding families and communities together.

So today, alongside celebration, I’m asking us to pause and think of them. To notice. To care. And to stand with women who are still fighting for safety, dignity and opportunity.

Happy International Women's Day to all.

Last year, Azam and I started noticing something unexpected in how colleagues at Thomson Reuters were talking about AI, and the use cases we were capturing in feedback. We expected to find the usual efficiency gains, time saved and tasks done faster, and we did. But people were describing work they simply couldn't have done before, taking on genuinely new capabilities and scaling up the ambition of what they were willing to attempt. Interestingly, often this was not displacing work that would have happened elsewhere but scaling up high value work. We structured feedback from hundreds of colleagues to understand what was actually changing and where the real value was coming from. We saw examples of business analysts with no coding background creating interactive visualizations and performing sophisticated data analyses. And non-technical programme managers automating reporting pipelines and creating dashboards. A few months on, the pattern is only getting stronger and we're seeing it right across the organisation, with people expanding the work they are capable of beyond their traditional role boundaries. So much of the narrative around AI focuses on headcount and cost reduction. I think we're missing the bigger story, which is about what happens when AI expands what people can do, not just how efficiently they do it. Last Friday afternoon, I was pulling CAC data across ten premium DTC brands for a benchmark I’m putting together. All have an AOV above $80. Some are early scale brands. Some are doing well over $20M in annual revenue. Going in, I assumed CAC would climb with revenue. That's the founder anxiety I hear on probably every other call. "We can't push spend yet, our CAC will spike when we scale." So I expressed CAC as a multiple of AOV so the comparison actually meant something. Then I plotted it. Median at the smallest tier: about 0.11x. Median at $5M to $20M: about 0.27x. Median at $20M+: about 0.36x. You're looking at that thinking "Tris, it does climb." And on the medians, sure. But look at the spread. The ranges overlap completely. One of the $20M+ brands runs at 0.35x. One of the smaller brands runs at 0.62x. The biggest brand on the chart pays less per customer, as a fraction of AOV, than half the brands below $5M. Revenue tier doesn't predict CAC. Category and AOV do. A premium home brand at $8M pays roughly what a premium home brand at $25M pays. Give or take. A consumable brand at $20M pays a fraction of what a jewellery brand at $5M. Almost every time. Look. If you're watching your CAC against your revenue and panicking when one climbs faster than the other, you're watching the wrong two numbers. That's the bit people miss. Pull your CAC against your AOV. What's your ratio? Genuinely curious how many of you have ever framed it that way.

Today is World Mental Health Day 🌎 . It’s a moment to pause and reflect on something that affects us all—our mental wellbeing.

This year’s theme, “Access to Services – Mental Health in Catastrophes and Emergencies”, reminds us that mental health support is not a luxury—it’s essential, especially in times of crisis.

The bombardment and mental toll of wars, natural disasters, personal loss, and the uncertainty and complexity of daily life are omnipresent.


Did you know?
1 in 8 people globally live with a mental health condition.
After major disasters, up to 30% of survivors may experience depression, anxiety, or PTSD.
At work, 51% of employees fear that speaking about mental health could harm their career.

But we also know—because research has shown—that every conversation, every act of kindness, every moment of listening can make a difference.
I want to help others regain their sparkle, feel safe to say “I’m not okay,” and find ways to access the support they need. This is what building a culture of care is all about.

Because behind every title, every frown, and every smile is a person who might just need an act of kindness and a moment of compassion.

If we all commit to checking in on one another, we’re more likely to catch each other when we fall.

### "Σε λατρεύω, η μαμά σου"

Η Έλλη Κοκκίνου γιόρτασε τα 18α γενέθλια του γιου της, Αλέξανδρου, με μια τρυφερή ανάρτηση και φωτογραφίες γεμάτες συναίσθημα - "Σε θαυμάζω και σε καμαρώνω", έγραψε

Μια πολύ συγκινητική ημέρα έζησε ηΈλλη Κοκκίνου, καθώς ο γιος της, Αλέξανδρος, έγινε 18 ετών. Η γνωστή τραγουδίστρια μοιράστηκε στα social media φωτογραφίες από διαφορετικές στιγμές της ζωής τους και συνόδευσε την ανάρτησή της με λόγια γεμάτα αγάπη, περηφάνια και μητρική συγκίνηση.

## Η Έλλη Κοκκίνου γιόρτασε την ενηλικίωση του γιου της

Η χθεσινή ημέρα είχε ξεχωριστή σημασία για την Έλλη Κοκκίνου, αφού ο γιος της, Αλέξανδρος, έκλεισε τα 18 του χρόνια και πέρασε επίσημα στην ενηλικίωση. Για τη γνωστή τραγουδίστρια, η στιγμή αυτή δεν ήταν απλώς ένα ακόμηγενέθλιο, αλλά ένα ορόσημο γεμάτο αναμνήσεις, συγκίνηση και περηφάνια. Με αφορμή τα γενέθλια του γιου της, η Έλλη Κοκκίνου δημοσίευσε φωτογραφίες από την κοινή τους διαδρομή, δείχνοντας στιγμές από τα παιδικά του χρόνια μέχρι σήμερα. Ανάμεσα στα στιγμιότυπα που ξεχώρισαν ήταν και μια φωτογραφία στην οποία ο Αλέξανδρος τη σηκώνει στους ώμους του, μια εικόνα που αποτυπώνει με τον πιο τρυφερό τρόπο το πέρασμα του χρόνου.

## Η ανάρτηση της Έλλης Κοκκίνου που συγκίνησε

Στη λεζάντα της ανάρτησής της, η τραγουδίστρια στάθηκε ακριβώς σε αυτή την αλλαγή των ρόλων, θυμούμενη την εποχή που εκείνη κρατούσε τον γιο της στην αγκαλιά της και βλέποντάς τον πλέον να έχει μεγαλώσει τόσο, ώστε να μπορεί εκείνος να τη σηκώνει στους ώμους του. «Και κάπως έτσι πέρασαν τα χρόνια και πήγες 18! Από εκεί που σε άντεχαν οι ώμοι μου τώρα ούτε να το σκεφτώ… Μπορείς όμως εσύ και το χαίρομαι! Να έχεις μια υπέροχη ζωή και να είσαι υγιής και ευτυχισμένος αγόρι μου υπέροχο. Σε θαυμάζω και σε καμαρώνω. Να σε χαιρόμαστε. Σε λατρεύω! Η μαμά σου». Τα λόγια της Έλλης Κοκκίνου είχαν έντονο συναισθηματικό φορτίο, καθώς μέσα σε λίγες γραμμές κατάφερε να χωρέσει τη χαρά, τη συγκίνηση και την περηφάνια μιας μητέρας που βλέπει το παιδί της να μεγαλώνει.

An exciting moment for us at Standard Chartered with the launch of our first Agentic AI colleague-facing solution, focused on new-hire onboarding. This marks an important milestone in how we are using AI to improve our colleague’s experience by fundamentally redesigning how work gets done. 
 
By embedding AI, we are simplifying a complex journey, improving the experience for new joiners, and reducing onboarding effort for hiring managers by an estimated 35% of the time they would otherwise spend on these tasks. Crucially, humans remain firmly in the loop — working in partnership with AI, which takes on the repetitive and administrative coordination so colleagues can focus on judgement, problem‑solving, and human connection.
 
This approach is a direct response to what we have learned through our work on workforce and operating-model redesign. When AI is layered onto existing processes without redesigning the work, 95% of organisations see zero ROI from AI investments. By contrast, leading AI organisations are twice as likely to redesign workflows to deliberately integrate human and machine capabilities. These insights shaped our decision to breakdown jobs into tasks, deciding what should be done by humans versus machines, and rebuilding the workflow around that split. 
 
This points to a broader shift - jobs matter less than tasks and skills. As agentic AI application increases, the most valuable skills will be those that sit alongside technology, such as digital fluency, human-AI collaboration, and the ability to interpret and improve outcomes. That is why we are linking this work to our focus on skills of the future and Global Learning Week (which starts today), building capacity as we redesign work. 
 
There is opportunity for leaders to move beyond experimenting with AI, and to redesign the workforce within organisations where people and machines work together intentionally - not by accident. 
 
#FutureOfWork #AgenticAI #WorkforceTransformation

Renminbi (RMB) usage is expanding across trade settlement, funding and capital markets, reshaping how corporates think about currency strategy. 

As a cross-border Bank, Standard Chartered sits at the intersection of where this shift is happening — across Greater China, ASEAN, the Middle East, Africa and beyond. We've been present on the ground in these markets for decades, building the relationships, the expertise and the infrastructure that allow us to connect clients to opportunity across the corridors that matter most.

That's why we've published Renminbi in Motion for Corporates — a report that moves beyond the macro narrative to where it really matters for our clients: funding flexibility, payments resilience, liquidity management, and FX alignment in an increasingly multipolar financial system.

Here's the context that makes it essential reading right now. China represents roughly 15% of global trade, yet the RMB accounts for less than 3.1% of global payments and just 1.9% of global reserves. That structural gap is narrowing, and the drivers this time are durable — rooted in real-economy demand rather than short-term policy cycles.

The infrastructure to support this is firmly in place, liquidity pools are deepening, and onshore and offshore markets are becoming increasingly connected. For corporates with China-linked exposure, this is no longer a theoretical conversation — your supply chains, procurement flows and revenue streams are already embedded in Asia-centred trade networks, whether or not your treasury framework has caught up.

Helping our clients navigate exactly that kind of complexity — with the expertise, the network and the long-term commitment to the markets where they operate — is what Standard Chartered is here to do.
